text:
A couple years ago, Mikala Sposito applied for a work ethic scholarship from my foundation. She asked for $2,700.00 to help realize her dream of becoming a welder. (Actually, her first dream was to become an Olympian. As a kid, she excelled at horseback riding, dance, soccer, and track, but not quite at the Olympic level. So, Mikala adjusted her dream and focused on something within her reach. Precisely the kind of commonsense approach to making a living we try to encourage.) Toward that end, Mikala filled out the application, jumped through all the necessary hoops, and signed the S.W.E.A.T. Pledge, as all applicants must.

According to our internal ranking system, which is inherently subjective and relative to each batch of new applicants, Mikala scored a 94, and was awarded $2,100.00, or roughly 80% of what she asked for. This is typical of the average percentage awarded to an excellent applicant. As a rule, we almost never award the entire amount requested. We want our recipients to have some skin in the game, and we encourage all applicants to apply for additional scholarship funds elsewhere, which Mikala did. But in this case, if I had it to do over again, I think I’d have awarded Mikala the full $2,700.00. Why? Because this woman is precisely why I award work ethic scholarships in the first place, as recent headlines prove. Headlines all over the country that identify Mikala Sposito as the sole welder to represent Team USA in the upcoming @WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai.

This is a very big deal. The World Skills competition is often referred to as the Olympics of the skilled trades, so it looks like Mikala’s dream is coming true after all. And it seems to me her journey is worth a brief encapsulation. Before she applied for a scholarship from mikeroweWORKS, Mikala demonstrated an affinity for welding in SkillsUSA. As a senior at Dexter High School, she won 1st Place at the SkillsUSA Michigan high school competition and went on to place 14th nationally. Then, as a freshman at Washtenaw Community College, she repeated her success by taking 1st Place in the Michigan college division. She then advanced to nationals, where she finished 8th in the country. That earned her an invitation to the Team USA pre-trials, which whittled the nation's top 16 young welders down to three. At the final USA Weld Trials at the Robotics Technology Park in Huntsville, Alabama, each competitor was evaluated on precision, safety, technical execution, craftsmanship, and multi-process capabilities under extreme time constraints. Mikala Sposito took the Gold, officially becoming the first woman to represent the United States in welding at WorldSkills. Next week, she’ll face off against the absolute best of the best from all over the world.

I should point out that Mikala would prefer it if the press didn’t make a big deal of her gender, and I completely understand. (She’s a welder – not a “weld-her.”) But today, the industry is in desperate need of proof that women can and do excel in the trades. Nationally, just 4.3% of tradespeople are female. At mikeroweWORKS, our female applicants are closer to 20%, but I assure you that percentage could be much higher. Companies are anxious to recruit talented welders of any gender, and women need to understand and believe the opportunities are real. Mikala prove that in spades, and I want to offer her my sincere congratulations, and invite all of you to do the same. Because Mikala Sposito is exactly what our country needs a lot more of. People who understand that talent is never enough to compensate for laziness.

In her application, she wrote, “Hard work beats talent any day of the week, and nobody is going to outwork me. Period.”

She also connected with every point of the S.W.E.A.T. Pledge but said the final tenet resonated with her the most. “Some people choose to be lazy. Some people choose to sleep in. I choose to work my butt off.”
My favorite quote, however, is Mikala’s response to seasoned professionals who see her wield a torch and call her a “natural.”

“I’m not a natural,” she says. Far from it. And none of this came easy. I worked and trained 60-80 hours a week for two years to get here.”

Regardless of what happens in Shanghai, the job offers are already piling up, including the most recent from SpaceX. She hasn’t graduated yet, but the future looks bright, and I for one would not bet against her.

PS. I never do this, but since my name is in the title of the foundation, I suppose I can. Mikala – please accept the additional $600 you requested from mikeroweWORKS two years ago. Shanghai is expensive, and since you’re representing all of us, we’d like to provide you with a little walking around money. The check is in the mail.

Now…go get the gold!

text:
Ahmad Ibsais on Aljazeera:

“Recent progressive wins of outspoken Israel critics in Democratic primaries have generated a lot of optimism. Abdul El-Sayed won the Dem nomination for a Senate seat in Michigan after AIPAC + its allies spent more than $54m against him in what came to be the most expensive Dem Senate primary in US history.

“In NJ, a surgeon named Adam Hamawy, who as a medical volunteer refused to leave Gaza until last member of his team could evacuate, won a 12-person primary in a House of Reps race.

“Years ago, such breakthroughs would have seemed impossible. For many on the left, it now seems like their hard work at the grassroots level is paying off.

“And yet, all the talk of a “shift on Israel” within the Dem Party is premature. The Dem establishment remains firmly in the Israeli camp, even if it is striking a more critical tone ahead of midterm elections. We should not mistake election-season displays of sympathy for a human-rights awakening on Palestine.

“We have now reached a point where the shift in attitudes towards Israel can no longer be ignored. A May poll by New York Times/Siena suggested that nearly 3/4 of Dem voters did not approve of aid for Israel. Another survey by Quinnipiac Univ showed that 66% of Dems thought US was too supportive of Israel. A poll published in April by Pew Research found that 80% of Dems viewed Israel unfavourably – up from 53% in 2022.

“These numbers have made the Dem leadership realise that open support for genocidaires is becoming too costly politically. Dem voters, who watched a livestreamed genocide, clearly no longer see Palestine as a secondary issue in their political and moral choices.
…

“But enough Dem Representatives still voted with Republican majority against it. The vote was politically useful precisely because it was powerless. The 103 Dem votes in favour of cutting aid to Israel gave the party something to campaign on, while ensuring Israel still had weapons it needs to continue its brutality.

“It is a strategy that the party is likely to repeat in next Congress to secure Israeli interests while appearing to acknowledge voters’ demands.

“Furthermore, the Dem establishment has shown little interest in breaking its dependence on AIPAC. In April, the Dem National Committee rejected even a symbolic resolution condemning the lobby’s interference in Dem primaries.

“AIPAC, meanwhile, has responded to its growing toxicity by learning how to disappear. Its super PAC has routed millions thru other orgs whose funding is disclosed only after voters cast their ballots. It has also directed donors through candidate-specific portals that leave individual names, rather than AIPAC’s, in public campaign records.

“Having spent more than $100m on this midterm race, AIPAC will continue to influence Dem congressional politics to ensure it is in favour of Israeli government.
…

“Rep Ro Khanna, for example, has been calling for aid cuts to Israel and an end to financing for the Iron Dome. He even went on a visit to occupied West Bank where he witnessed settler violence firsthand.

“Even then, standing before the Dem National Committee earlier this month and calling for zero aid to Israel, he led with the disclaimer that Hamas’s attack must be condemned unequivocally. He still refuses to say that Palestinians have the right to self-defence.

“Brad Lander, who won NY primary for a House seat in June and was backed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has described what is happening in Gaza as genocide. +yet, his criticism goes only that far. He identifies as “liberal Zionist”+has made clear he does not support BDS.

“Prominent progressives like Bernie Sanders+AOC , who are already in Congress, have also demonstrated they can only offer a partial solidarity w/Palestinian people – one that does not acknowledge their status+rights as occupied people.
…

… “We must reject every attempt by Dem Party to pay lip service to our cause; we must continue to push for real action on Israel.”

text:
A RATE RISE IS TWO PRICES AT ONCE - AND RAYMOND JAMES $RJF IS PAYING BOTH:

Raymond James Financial, ticker RJF, at $163.77 (after hours), -$0.80 / -0.49% today. Fifth of sixty-five on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5. The St. Petersburg, Florida firm has put financial advisers in front of American households since 1962.

On Wednesday the Federal Reserve raised its target range - the rate banks charge each other overnight - a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase since 2023, with consumer prices running 3.4% above a year earlier. Every company on this board that earns its living on the price of money fell that afternoon, and all four are still lower tonight. The two here with no interest-rate business are both higher.

An interest rate is not one price. It is two - what a company earns on money, and what it has to pay for money - and Wednesday moved both at once. The only question for a so-called rate winner is which side is bigger. One name below put its answer in writing.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
GitLab at $50.20 (after hours), +$1.43 / +2.93% today. Seventh of thirty. The San Francisco company hosts the code software teams ship. This Len5 wants a price near its one-year high with both climbs agreeing: +168% from the April 10 low of $18.73, but 9.6% under the $55.55 high of September 2. The September 1 quarter built it - revenue $286.3M, +21%. Its rate answer is the rare happy one: a $56.9M operating loss came out as a $36.8M net loss, and that $20.1M of difference is made below the operating line, where interest on $1.26B of cash sits. CHANGE IT: its own map for this quarter is $281M-$283M, under the $286.3M just delivered. WHEN: December 1, tentative. VERDICT: the only name here collecting the new rate instead of paying it, and the only one guiding next quarter lower.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
The Hartford Insurance Group at $133.14 (after hours), -$1.80 / -1.33% today. Fifth of fifty-seven. The 216-year-old Connecticut company insures businesses, cars and homes. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth - here 1.9 times the net worth on its own books. On July 23 investment income printed $800M against $658M, which reads as higher rates arriving. Strip out limited partnerships, $114M against $13M on real-estate venture sales, and the rest grew 6% - on more money invested, the company said, not a better yield. Reported profit jumped 31%; core profit, earnings with one-off items stripped, rose 1%. CHANGE IT: investment income growing on yield rather than size. WHEN: October 26, tentative. VERDICT: a fine underwriter whose best line last quarter was a property sale.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Raymond James again, and the one with it in writing. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply. Settled: $1.922 trillion of client money under administration at June 30, +17%, and a record $3.928B of net revenues in the June quarter, reported July 22, earning $3.01 a share, +42%. Cheap: about 14 times the last year of profit from a firm earning 18.8% on its owners' equity.

The deciding number is $58.8B - client cash in sweep and Enhanced Savings accounts, up 7% on the year. A higher Fed rate lifts what that cash earns and what Raymond James pays to keep it: here the depositor is the client. Which side moved is on the record. Enhanced Savings balances, the higher-paying option, jumped 19% in three months as clients chose it; the margin the bank earns on lending fell 10 basis points to 2.71%; and bank net interest income came out flat, loan growth cancelled by the interest paid on those balances.

CHANGE IT: it guided that combined $658M roughly flat again this quarter, "based on static interest rates." Rates then moved, inside the last fortnight of that quarter. WHEN: October 28 after the close, confirmed, $3.24 carried against $3.11. VERDICT: a record wealth manager at 14 times earnings, marked down 10.4% from its August 6 high by the one event most would file under good news.

GROWTH LEN5:
Ameris Bancorp at $83.00 (after hours), -$0.72 / -0.86% today. Sixth of thirty. The Atlanta bank lends across the Southeast and writes home loans. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and the June quarter, reported July 23, is the two prices cancelling inside one company. Lending: net interest income $253.4M against $232.7M, +8.9%. Fees: mortgage income $32.5M against $39.2M, -17.1%, as the spread it keeps on selling a loan slipped to 2.04% from 2.22%. Net of the two, adjusted profit was $1.60 a share against $1.59 - flat, and its first miss of the published expectation in eight quarters. CHANGE IT: mortgage income steadying. WHEN: October 26, tentative. VERDICT: every loan earns more and every mortgage sells for less.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Nebius Group at $215.80 (after hours), +$6.43 / +3.07% today. Seventh of thirty. The Amsterdam company rents out AI computing - halls of Nvidia chips other firms pay for by the hour. This Len5 wants very fast growth on a base big enough to be real, and August 12 carried both: revenue $582.3M, +454% on the year, and a run rate - what its current pace works out to over a full year - of $3B. This morning it did what none of the others can: from October 1 it raises rental prices by up to 21%, the H200 chip going from $4.50 to $5.40 an hour, its second rise this year. CHANGE IT: it has guided $20B-$25B of building against $3.0B-$3.4B of revenue, and borrows to do it - on August 19 it priced $5B of convertible notes, 0.50% due 2030 and 4.50% due 2034. The cost of money is in that second number. WHEN: November 10, tentative. VERDICT: the only company here answering dearer money by raising its own price - and the market still took back three fifths of a 9.9% opening jump by the close.

INCOME LEN5:
Lincoln National at $42.01 (after hours), -$0.44 / -1.04% today. Eighth of thirty. The Radnor, Pennsylvania company sells life insurance, annuities and workplace benefits. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself pays for. The cover is wide: $0.45 a quarter, $1.80 a year, about 4.3% of today's price, against $2.24 of adjusted operating profit per share in the June quarter - a fifth of it. Higher rates should be the gift: two thirds of sales are spread products, where Lincoln keeps the gap between what its investments earn and what it pays the saver. CHANGE IT: the same rate hands every customer a better offer elsewhere - balances hit a record $182B, and the book still lost about $2.9B more than it took in. WHEN: October 29 before the open, tentative. VERDICT: the widest cover here, funded by savings that shrank in the quarter they earned most.

Every forecast here was written before Wednesday. Raymond James wrote its own on a stated assumption - static interest rates - and the rate moved in the last fortnight of the quarter it covers. The four companies here paid in interest all report within four days of each other at the end of October. None will get to show the earning half without the paying half attached.

Not investment advice.

text:
The problem is that there are no good analysts in the United States who truly understand Russia and understand what is happening there. And it is not only Ian who lacks such analysts; the intelligence services do as well. This is clearly visible from the way events are unfolding.
 🚫There Is No Alternative. 🚫

A historical moment in which there is, in essence, no alternative to the Kremlin.

This is Russia’s main advantage over America and China today.

Many people fail to grasp this, which leads to faulty analysis and empty expectations of either another 1917 or another 1991, when people brought down an Empire for the sake of an IDEA.

After all, 1917 and 1991 did not happen simply because there was a crisis. A crisis by itself does not bring down Empires from within. To destroy an empire, there must be a second component alongside the crisis, and that is an Alternative Idea, a New Path.

There was an alternative path in 1917. The Socialist Revolutionaries had their social democracy, while the Bolsheviks had their own new path in the form of communism. And in 1991, during the collapse of the Soviet Empire, there was not only a crisis, but also an alternative new path offered by the democrats in the form of democracy and the market.

So a Crisis is, of course, a necessary condition, but not a sufficient one. Without the second factor, the product equals zero.

But when it comes to new alternative Ideas, Russia is currently in very bad shape. And this is largely the result of the historical moment, not the absence of strong new leaders.

This can be clearly seen in America today, for example, where very weak, and often simply foolish, people advocating the construction of socialism in America enjoy broad support. This shows that what matters most is still the Idea, because even a very strong leader cannot rally the masses behind an unpopular idea. But when the Idea exists, when society sees an alternative, it is prepared to follow even very weak and foolish leaders.

The peak moment comes when there is a new Path that many people want to follow, and at the same time a strong Leader, a tribune, appears.

As happened in history, for example, with Hitler.

The highest point of danger for a system is a historical convergence: a living Idea combined with a strong, charismatic tribune and leader, exactly as happened in Germany at that time.

Hitler, after all, did not force upon all Germans something they did not want. He gave them precisely what they wanted at the time, or at least what many of them wanted. He implemented exactly the program on which he had campaigned for power. He did not deceive his voters.

He had also offered them that same war from the beginning. From the outset, he spoke about expansion, and expansion was one of the central goals of the Path.

When people are not attracted by an Idea and its Leader, they will not voluntarily go to war as an entire country, especially when the war is not defensive but offensive. Nor will they fight a bloody war until the very end, all the way to the Reichstag.

America now has a new popular Idea, but it has no popular leader, no vivid and charismatic tribune capable of uniting the masses who are searching for an alternative and a new path. For now, this allows us not to worry too much about this new idea coming to power. But the Idea will not die either. It will continue to smolder and, depending on the situation in the country, its support will either increase or decrease. The Idea will remain alive and wait for its Leader, someone capable of bringing it to power.

An Idea does not die in the absence of a tribune. It lies dormant, breathes with the situation in the country, expands and contracts, and waits.

Socialism in America is like a smoldering peat bog: there is no open blaze, but the fire continues to spread underground. The only question is when the wind will appear, in the form of a strong tribune, a brilliant, intelligent and charismatic leader.

Another scenario is also possible, in which even an uncharismatic leader could bring socialism to power. But that would require an enormous internal crisis accompanied by total dissatisfaction among the majority.

This means that America faces two dangerous scenarios, not one. Either a tribune appears at the current level of dissatisfaction, or no tribune appears, but the crisis becomes total, in which case any gray socialist functionary will be enough. The second scenario is even more treacherous: everyone watches the charismatic figures, while systems are sometimes brought down by colorless functionaries.

America has a new path. Part of the population dislikes it, but that does not negate its existence.

China also has a new path, in the form of democracy as an attractive alternative to communism for many people.

And this is where Russia’s main advantage becomes apparent: because of the present historical moment, it has no Alternative.

Russia has already tried both of these ideas in its recent past, and in the eyes of many people, neither ended particularly well.

The inoculation against communism, with its tragic ending still fresh in this historical period, makes the ideas of social communism that are currently popular in America unable to take off in Russia. Even with a brilliant leader, this idea would not take off. History has not yet had enough time to whitewash it and make it attractive again in the eyes of many people.

Likewise, the new alternative idea of liberal democracy was also recently tried by the country, and its results were far from encouraging.

The wild 1990s are still remembered by many as difficult and lawless years, rather than as exciting and romantic ones.

The democrats of that period failed to understand that order was more important to the people than freedom. They therefore kept thinking about where they could provide even more freedom, instead of thinking about how to establish order in the country.

As a result, they created even greater disorder, because every form of order is built on restricting certain actions. You cannot give everyone complete freedom and still maintain order, because order consists of rules, and rules are restrictions in one form or another. Order must not simply impose restrictions; it must also inspire fear. People must be afraid to violate its rules and restrictions, because the more people are unafraid to break the rules of order and have no fear of them, the more order in a country shifts toward disorder, or toward an order that exists only for a privileged few.

In Russia during the 1990s, the democrats attacked order from two directions: by eliminating fear of violating the established order, and by giving absolute priority to every kind of freedom over the restrictions on which order depends.

That is why the 1990s were, in essence, such an anarchic period, when there was a great deal of freedom but very little order. And the majority of people are fed by order, not by freedom.

For an ordinary person, freedom without order is chaos in which the strongest or the most shameless survive.

This was what allowed Putin to defeat the liberal democrats in elections by contrasting his order with their disorder.

The liberal-democratic idea in Russia discredited itself, as did its leaders.

Or rather, the absence of such leaders. Yes, there was Nemtsov, and then there was Navalny, but their election results were, in essence, their real results, not the product of some enormous manipulation by the authorities.

They could make noise and bring part of the population into the streets, but they did not have the number of voters behind them required to win an election.

Navalny was as successful as he was largely because he was not as purely and visibly liberal-democratic as Nemtsov. He had emerged from a nationalist background. That was an advantage, not a disadvantage. He had more sides to him than Nemtsov, giving different kinds of voters something they could identify with and a reason to follow him.

But even that was not enough for Navalny to take power through elections, because there was no enormous crisis, and the Idea itself had not yet been rehabilitated after the 1990s.

The results achieved by Nemtsov and Navalny were not the product of manipulation. They were an almost honest measurement of the Idea multiplier. Making noise and bringing people into the streets is one thing: that is the energy of a minority. Elections measure the mass standing behind the Idea, and that mass was insufficient.

It was insufficient ten years ago, and it remains insufficient today. In addition, after Navalny’s departure, there are no new brilliant leaders. It is not simply that no brilliant new figures have emerged. Almost all of the older, well-known figures, even those who were never particularly brilliant, have politically buried themselves. Both those who left voluntarily and those whom Putin forced out, instead of simply campaigning for and supporting an end to the war, began supporting a Ukrainian victory. And the overwhelming majority of voters do not particularly like politicians who OPENLY support the opposing side against their own people during a war and celebrate destruction in their former Homeland.

The difference between “supporting an end to the war” and “supporting a Ukrainian victory” is the difference between a position from which it is theoretically possible to return to politics and a position that, in the eyes of the majority of voters, permanently removes you from the ranks of their own people.

The Idea is therefore not yet electorally viable, while brilliant leaders are completely absent. Or, more accurately, the existing leaders have been completely discredited.

It has turned out that, during this particular historical period, Russia has already suffered through the two main and largest alternative “new” ideas in the world, and for the moment it retains immunity to both of them.

The majority of voters currently sees neither social communism nor liberal democracy as an attractive alternative.

It is therefore foolish to expect what some experts predict when they anticipate either another 1917 or another 1991 in Russia.

These ideas will not work now, and even strong leaders would not be able to carry them to victory.

And today, there are no other major ideas in the world besides Islam and the right-wing movement.

Putinism itself is, in essence, a right-wing movement by modern standards, limited only by how far to the right it can move within a multiethnic Empire without destroying that Empire from within.

There is, in fact, no alternative to Putinism. It cannot be outflanked from the right either. It may be softer or harsher, but today, in the eyes of the majority of voters, there is no real alternative to it.

Even the Trumpian alternative path of returning to a golden and glorious past is currently impossible in Russia because there is no image of such a golden past.

This is a new Empire. It is only thirty-five years old, so it physically cannot yet have a golden past, especially since the formation of an Empire is almost always a turbulent and bloody period.

Because of America’s age, it has a past to which it can return, and it has periods that can be sold to many people as golden years. Russia, because of its much shorter past, simply does not have such a period.

Nor is it realistic to sell the majority the golden age of the former Russian empires, whether communist or tsarist, and lead people in great columns toward that bright past.

There is probably only one version of the past that can be sold in Russia: a return to the prewar period, before the war in Ukraine. But even that would still be Putin’s time, a return to Putin’s Russia, simply in a softer form.

And to return there, Russia would essentially have to admit defeat in the war, which completely contradicts the nature of Putin’s Russia. That is precisely what makes a return to that period unrealistic.

The door into the golden past appears to exist, but it can be opened only with a key that destroys the very past waiting behind that door.

Russia now finds itself in a very rare historical situation in which, in essence, there are no real alternative paths.

And here we return once again to Hitler. He also found himself in a historical period when, for a huge part of society, all the other major paths had already been burned out or discredited.

For the Germans, Weimar democracy was a spent alternative. It was associated with Versailles, hyperinflation, humiliation and unemployment. In addition, after the disorder of democracy, Hitler genuinely restored order to the country and improved the lives of the majority. This drove another nail into the coffin of the liberal-democratic idea. The Germans had been inoculated against it. Meanwhile, the majority had been inoculated against communism by the USSR, through the actions taking place inside the Soviet Empire at the time, multiplied further by Western anti-communist propaganda.

In other words, the Germans initially turned to Nazism partly because, in their eyes, the other paths had already been burned out. No new paths emerged before the end of the war, while the enemy’s demands for capitulation only forced the Germans to close ranks around the Idea and the leader they had chosen. This played a role in their endurance and in their genuine resistance all the way to the Reichstag.

The ending of the First World War was not repeated. At that time, domestic political instability caused by the emergence and growth of new, popular internal alternative ideas forced the authorities to capitulate in a war that had not even crossed Germany’s borders and was still being fought outside its territory.

This is where the similarity lies between the present condition of the Russian Empire and the Third Reich. There are no real alternatives attractive to the majority of voters. Or rather, such alternatives exist, but society has been inoculated against them, and there are neither effective Ideas nor brilliant leaders to represent them.

A Crisis is merely fuel. Without an engine, the Idea, and ignition, the Leader, the vehicle of revolution will not move.

When there are no great, brilliant and attractive Ideas, and no new leaders either, even an internal crisis does not lead to the fall of the regime.

Toward the end of its existence, the Roman Empire was also in a state of permanent crisis, but it truly collapsed only after an external conquest.

Until that external conquest occurred, the crisis merely changed the leaders rather than the system itself.

The same applies to Russia. An enormous crisis may lead only to Putin being replaced, not to the end of Putinism, because there are no major alternative Ideas.

Russia today is protected not so much by the strength of its repressive apparatus as by a unique historical moment. Over the course of a single century, the lifetime of three generations, the country has tested the two most powerful systemic alternatives that currently exist:

The communist project ended in shortages, cynicism and the geopolitical collapse of 1991.

The liberal-democratic project ended in poverty, gangsterism, the loss of stability and the humiliation of the 1990s.

Putinism itself is not so much an ideology as a functional model.

It is based on a combination of a strong state, order, patriotism, great-power identity and relative social stability compared with the 1990s.

At the same time, it is flexible. Harshness, isolation and pragmatism are controls on a panel that can be turned in either direction depending on the circumstances. The main elements are the vertical power structure and order. They form the body of the system.

Today, it cannot be attacked from the position of the past, because the past has been discredited, or from the position of the future, because the future is blurred and undefined.

As for whether Putinism can be ended through the military conquest of the new Russian Empire, with its nuclear weapons and such a past behind it, everyone can answer that question for themselves.

The same formula also works in reverse.

It explains why, despite all the problems in Ukraine’s the home front, that the home front has not yet collapsed. A crisis and a war by themselves are not enough to change the country’s course under the simple slogan “we want peace.” There must also be an alternative Idea built around peace and a brilliant Leader to represent it.

Mass dissatisfaction takes shape around an alternative Idea, not simply around the desire to “live normally.”

A Crisis produces dissatisfaction, but only an Idea transforms dissatisfaction into power.

Dissatisfaction is a condition. It is dispersed like steam: it presses in every direction at once and therefore presses nowhere.

Only form can turn it into power, and the Idea provides that form.

The demand to “live normally” offers no answer to the question of exactly how people should live. It offers no program, no enemy and no vision of tomorrow. Consequently, it offers no point around which people can unite. For one person, “normal” means low prices; for another, freedom; for a third, order; and for a fourth, the return of the past. A million dissatisfied people, each with a different idea of what “normal” means, are not yet a force. They are a million isolated individuals.

An Idea begins where a million individual declarations of “I’ve had enough” are transformed into a single collective statement: “Instead of this, we want this.”

Dispersed steam is merely dampness. But collect it inside a boiler, build up its pressure and direct it into a piston, and it will move an entire train.

The Idea is precisely the form that transforms dispersed dissatisfaction into a MOVEMENT.

text:
The Setpoint, Not the Spark

What intention might be, what it probably never was, and what a working practitioner can honestly do with the difference.

The inherited model fits on a candle. You form an intent, you concentrate, you charge it, you release it, and then the packet is out in the world. Results come or they do not, and the standard postmortem says the charge was weak, the gnosis shallow, or the operator lusted after the result. Most working groups still run some version of this, including groups that consider themselves traditional, and the entire manifestation industry is the same architecture with the ritual furniture removed.

That architecture is the same one that volition research has spent roughly twenty years dismantling in its scientific form: perception, then decision, then action, with a discrete willing event somewhere in the middle. If the science moved, the practitioner's model moved with it, whether or not anyone in the craft noticed, because both were running the same diagram. That is the honest reason this is worth a practitioner's attention. It is not that neuroscience has anything to say about whether a working works.

Start with what the experiments actually left standing, because the popular version of this story is wrong in both directions. The measurement was never in doubt. Brain activity does precede reported awareness of the intention to move, and that has been reproduced many times. What collapsed was the inference from it, and it collapsed for three reasons that do not depend on each other. The pre-movement signal may be substantially an artifact of averaging trials backward from the moment of movement, which is Schurger's account from 2012. The signal largely disappears when the choice is deliberate rather than arbitrary, which is Maoz and colleagues from 2019, and which matters more than anything else in the literature, because finger-lifting was never the interesting case. And the discrete decision moment the old story presupposed may not correspond to anything in the motor system at all, which is the live argument now. The social psychology built downstream of the old story, the studies claiming that disbelief in free will makes people cheat, has largely failed to replicate under preregistration, and a 2023 meta-analysis found no evidence for downstream effects.

Two things are in slightly better shape than the harsh debunking allowed, and both come from specific paradigms and should be held that way. Subjects in one 2016 study could still cancel a prepared movement quite late in the process, later than the old story implied, which is evidence that interruption is real in that task rather than proof that a general veto faculty exists. And a 2026 study using a typing task with random probes found that awareness of what one was about to type arrived more than a second before the act, with a corresponding neural signature, and its authors concluded that this is hard to square with treating the experience of intention as pure retrospective invention. That is their conclusion from one study with fifty one participants across two experiments, only one of which recorded brain activity. It is suggestive. It is not settled.

Now the part the draft got wrong, and it is the load-bearing part. None of this established that the organism is best described as a bank of control loops holding variables at setpoints. That is a framework, associated with perceptual control theory and with the paper that put the diagram on the thumbnail, and it is one contender among several, including predictive processing and optimal feedback control, which differ in ways that matter. What the collapse of the old inference does is make room for such pictures by removing the obligation to find the moment where the decision happened. Room is not vindication. If you build a practice on the control picture, you are betting on a framework, and you should know that you are betting.

And nothing here touches determinism. Neuroscience never had a claim on whether you could have done otherwise in the strict metaphysical sense, and it still does not. What it can measure is control, interruption, the setting of references, and prospective awareness. What it cannot measure is freedom in the sense people want when they want an exemption from causal structure, because nobody has said what would have to be true in the tissue for it to be absent. That is a definitional problem, not an experimental one, and no amount of further scanning will touch it.

On the history, resist the version where the ancients had it right and the moderns coarsened it. That story is available and it is too clean. Binding tablets, coercive compulsion of spirits, and operations that launch something at a named target are as old as the documentary record gets, and the Greek magical papyri are not shy about it. What is recent is not projection. What is recent is the psychologized version of projection, in which the thing projected is a mental state of the operator rather than a name, a substance, or a god's compulsion. That shift is roughly Victorian in its modern form, it runs through the Golden Dawn's training of visualization and vibration into a will you raise and send, and it becomes method in the second half of the twentieth century, with the sigil compressed and discharged at a peak state and then deliberately forgotten. New Thought supplied the ambient version that everyone now breathes. So when a contemporary practitioner says intention is everything, the phrase is carrying about a hundred and fifty years, not three thousand, and what it carries specifically is the assumption that the operative thing is a mental event occurring at a moment.

Crowley is the interesting case, because the prohibition on lust of result sits awkwardly inside that architecture. A ban on staring at the outcome is not what you would expect from a theory in which the discharge is the whole event. I will not tell you he recognized a control-theoretic fact, because I have no way to know what he recognized and claiming otherwise would be the kind of retrospective flattery that makes this genre unreadable. What I will say is that the ban converges with something a control picture predicts, and convergence is worth noticing even when you cannot explain it.

Here is the mapping, offered as an analogy and not as a result, because analogies between cybernetics and ritual are cheap and the cheapness is exactly why this one has to be labelled. Suppose intention is a maintained reference rather than a discharged packet. Then what carries weight is persistence of a setpoint across time and disturbance, not intensity at a moment, and practices that train peak states would be training a different variable, which may still be useful for interrupting a stuck pattern but is not how a reference is held. Then the ban on lust of result reads as mechanical rather than pious, since conscious monitoring of a controlled variable destabilizes correction the way attending to your feet destabilizes walking, and banishing in order to forget reads as taking your hands off the manual override. Then the attention some practitioners give to the texture of being about to act is attention to something with a measurable signature rather than to a stitched-on illusion. Every one of those sentences begins with suppose. None of them is evidence that any practice works.

Which brings me to the part I am actually confident about, and it is the part that needs no neuroscience at all. The practical advice that falls out of this framing is good advice on ordinary grounds, and you should take it for those grounds rather than because a diagram from a journal endorsed it.

Name the variable you will not let drift, and name it as a state rather than as an outcome. Answering correspondence the same day is a variable. Being someone people can rely on is a mood. The test is whether you can say what the disturbance looks like; if you cannot describe what would count as drift, you do not have a reference yet. Train the unspectacular correction rather than the ordeal, on the grounds that the ordeal may change a reference and the following forty days are what hold it. Treat interruption as part of the working rather than as failure, since noticing that the loop has been hijacked and putting the reference back is the skill, and banishing as a living practice rather than a script is exactly that. Allow references to be revised by argument and not only by getting burned, because a will that cannot survive contact with a good objection is a habit with incense attached. Once the reference is set, make the next disturbance the object of attention rather than the scoreboard. And keep a log of references rather than a log of manifestations: what you set, what disturbed it, what correction you made, whether you revised the reference and on what grounds. That log is the practice, and it has the additional virtue of being the only version of this that can tell you afterward whether anything changed.

Now the limit, which I would not soften for anyone. All of the above concerns where intention lives inside the agent. It says nothing whatever about the extrospective claim. If your operative model is that intention reaches past the skin and moves events directly, this shift gives you nothing, and the stronger reading of the James argument makes your position worse rather than better, because on that reading intention does not even cause your own arm to move in the way the packet theory wanted. A practice that treats will as an outward efficient cause of weather, lovers, and hiring committees gains no ground here. If psi exists it will have to be argued from evidence of its own, and it must not be smuggled back in under the word intention on the strength of a diagram about motor control.

What does gain is the reading many capable practitioners already hold when they are being straight about it, which is that the working operates on the operator. If the locus of the craft is the reference values of your own loops, meaning what you attend to, what registers as a disturbance worth correcting, and what you refuse to let drift, then the craft is working on precisely the variables this picture identifies as the agency-bearing ones. That is not a consolation prize, and it is the part of the traditional claim that survives contact.

So the doctrine that intention is the most important part of the craft is nearly right or badly wrong depending on which sense of the word is in play, and the craft has not noticed that it changed senses. If intention means the maintained reference plus the attentional regime that serves it, the doctrine is close to a statement about how control systems are thought to work, and the word has been carrying an enormous amount quietly. If it means the spark, the charge, and the release at the moment of the working, then the doctrine borrowed an architecture that has been coming apart for twenty years in the one field that was testing it, and the borrowing is worth noticing whatever you conclude about it.

You can keep the word. Be honest about which machine it names.

text:
We’re approaching our holiday season. Please, remember our vets. It’s important.🇺🇸

From a buddy. Pass it on. 

“If you have a combat veteran in your family and you don’t like their moods/behavior around the holidays, please consider these six things:   

1) Your combat veteran has served in countries where people are blessed to receive a tattered pair of shoes or have clean water to drink; he/she no longer lives the “first world illusion” and no longer cares that if you buy one play station you can get a second one for fifty percent off. In fact, they find it hard to appreciate any of the gluttonous commercialism and overindulgence that permeates American holidays. Standing watch, boring as it was, had so much more purpose than going to the mall. 

2) Your combat veteran is thankful for the most basic things; not thankful for mega-sales and million dollar parades. They are thankful to be alive; thankful to have survived both the wars far away and the wars they struggle with inside. 

3) Your combat veteran is thankful that it wasn't them that got killed, but their celebrations are forever complicated by guilt and loss over those that were. Some of the most thankful times in their life were some of the scariest. Their feelings of thanks and celebration often conjure memories that are equally painful. 

4) Your combat veteran is not like you anymore. At some point, for some period of time, their entire life boiled down to just three simple things: when will I eat today, when will I sleep today, and who will I have to kill or will try to kill me today? They are not like you anymore.  

5) Your combat veteran does not need a guilt-trip or a lecture; they already feel detached in their grief while others so easily embrace the joy of the season. They need understanding and space; empathy not sympathy.

6.) Your combat veteran does love his/her family and is thankful for the many blessings in their life…and they are thankful for you.”

To all my brothers and sisters of the uniform, know that we all struggle with one thing or another but as we go into this holiday season, reach out to those you love. You didn't fight alone on the battlefield and we don't have to fight alone at home…

And remember;  Holidays are especially critical times for us to conduct "Buddy checks" with our veteran friends and their families.

God Bless....🙏

🔎 The tool: The Federal Register, operated by the National Archives, briefly offered an AI-powered search feature using Alibaba’s Qwen model, a Chinese-developed AI system, to help users search proposed federal regulations. 

🇨🇳 Why it drew scrutiny: The FBI had recently accused Alibaba of maliciously copying technology from Anthropic, adding a striking national-security dimension to the discovery. The allegations concern Chinese developers obtaining and using outputs from U.S. frontier AI systems to help develop their own models. 

🗑️ It was removed: Reuters found that the Qwen-powered search option was available Wednesday but was taken down later that day, around the time social-media posts drew attention to its presence. Reuters also reviewed archived source code confirming the tool's deployment. 

🛡️ Security question: Experts noted that the situation is more nuanced than simply saying Chinese AI was given access to sensitive government information. Qwen is an open-weight model, and the Federal Register's underlying material is public. However, security concerns depend in part on where the AI processing occurred and whether Alibaba-controlled infrastructure handled any user or government data. 

⚠️ The broader contradiction: The episode highlights a tension in U.S. policy: Washington has been warning government agencies and companies about risks associated with Chinese AI technology while a federal website was simultaneously deploying a Chinese model. Senator Mark Warner said the security assessment would depend heavily on how the system was architected and what data, if any, was sent to Alibaba-controlled systems. 

🇺🇸🇨🇳 Timing matters: The incident comes just before an expected Trump-Xi meeting, making the use of Alibaba's technology particularly sensitive amid escalating U.S.-China competition over advanced AI.

⚛️ Major federal competition: The U.S. Department of Energy launched the Quantum Genesis Q Competition on September 17, offering up to $215 million to private-sector companies pursuing the first fault-tolerant, scientifically relevant quantum computer. 

🧮 The target: DOE wants a machine with at least 100 logical qubits capable of performing hundreds of millions of reliable, fault-tolerant operations—a much higher bar than simply having a large number of physical qubits. 

💰 How the money is structured: Phase I offers milestone awards of up to $1.5 million per awardee. Phase II has a $100 million pool for systems reaching 100 logical qubits, plus $50 million bonuses for reaching 150 and 200 logical qubits. 

🔬 What it could solve: DOE is specifically targeting problems that are currently beyond practical classical computing, including chemistry, materials science, physics and applied mathematics. Potential applications include new materials, batteries, superconductors and fusion-energy research. 

📅 2028 is the target: The broader Quantum Genesis initiative aims to demonstrate scientifically relevant fault-tolerant systems in 2028, with logical-qubit counts in the low hundreds. 

🏢 Private companies are being asked to compete: Applications are open to domestic commercial entities, including both large companies and small businesses. Applications are due October 19, 2026. 

⚠️ Still a major technical challenge: The goal is not simply to build a bigger quantum computer. Quantum systems currently suffer from errors that accumulate during calculations; fault tolerance and error correction are what would make long, scientifically useful computations reliable. The DOE competition is therefore aimed at crossing a fundamental technological threshold, not merely increasing qubit counts.

Huntington Beach is making history.
 
Huntington Beach is the first destination in California to earn Sensory Inclusive® Certification from KultureCity, recognizing the community’s commitment to creating a more welcoming and supportive experience for people with sensory needs and invisible disabilities.
 
Today, we celebrated this milestone with a special KultureCity certification and celebratory ceremony at Huntington Beach Pier Plaza, bringing together City leaders, Visit Huntington Beach, KultureCity, community partners, and tourism businesses that helped make this citywide initiative possible.
 
This effort goes beyond a certification. Through training, resources, and partnerships, Huntington Beach is working to make sensory inclusion part of how we serve residents and visitors throughout the community.
 
• 95% of City employees have completed KultureCity sensory-inclusive training, exceeding certification requirements for public safety and other City departments.
• 100 sensory bags are available throughout City facilities, including City Hall, community centers, libraries, and select public safety and Code Enforcement vehicles. The bags include noise-reducing headphones, fidget toys, sunglasses, communication boards, and informational cards.
• More than 1,538 visitor-facing employees across hotels, restaurants, retail businesses, and attractions have completed the certification, extending sensory-inclusive practices throughout the visitor experience.
 
The training and resources give City employees and public safety personnel additional tools to recognize sensory sensitivities and better support individuals who may experience sensory overload, particularly during stressful or unfamiliar situations.
 
We’re proud to mark this important milestone and continue building a Huntington Beach where more people can participate, explore, and enjoy all our community has to offer.

100+ Flavor-Packed, Foolproof Recipes from My Asian American Kitchen

by Chris Joe 

Delivers by September 22 onwards

Chris Joe, creator of the beloved and reliable online platform  @cj. eats, dishes out tried and true recipes for classic Asian dishes

As a third-generation Chinese-American, Chris Joe grew up in Los Angeles enjoying wontons, roast duck, crispy pork belly, and more Asian classics with his family. From a young age, Chris learned first-hand the essential cooking techniques required to make these classic dishes from his grandparents, who settled in California as first-generation butchers and grocery store owners. After they had passed, Chris continued to study and practice those techniques, eventually devoting himself to learning the secrets behind the beloved dishes he grew up eating. 

Soon he’d perfected Egg Drop Soup (notoriously simple, but finnicky), hand-pulled noodles (intimidating, but do-able!), and even dishes inspired by his wife Kat’s Korean heritage like Korean Seafood Pancakes, or Haemul-pajeon. He mastered frying, velveting meats, folding dumplings, and more, and each recipe he conquered made him more confident and fearless in the kitchen. He wanted to inspire that feeling in others and began sharing his skills and his passion of Asian food on social media, and now has a huge and devoted audience of fans who love his approachable (and straight-forward) cooking style.   

In COOK ASIAN, Chris offers carefully crafted recipes and key tips (toss the noodles with oil before stir frying to prevent them from sticking!  Salt the cucumbers for a crispier, crunchier texture!) to make sure readers not only know the how of each step, but also the why. From an authentic Wonton Noodle Soup and Chicken Karaage to Korean BBQ Beef (Bulgogi) and Pad Thai, Chris demystifies complex recipes with straightforward steps, and a “no-advice-left-behind approach” to inspire readers to build their own cooking muscle, and make these irresistible dishes part of their life, too.

text:
My Recruiting Story

People ask me why I’m so passionate about helping athletes with recruiting.

The answer is simple—I lived it.

In 2007, I was blessed to receive opportunities from Mary Hardin-Baylor and Blinn College. But I was a lost young man. I wasn’t ready mentally, and I walked away from football.

Two years later, everything changed.

My mom passed away.

Three weeks later, on Mother’s Day, my first child was born.

Experiencing my greatest loss and my greatest blessing so close together changed my perspective forever. I realized life is too short to spend it wondering, “What if?”

I decided I was going to chase my dream again.

There was just one problem—I had been away from football for nearly two years. There was no transfer portal, no recruiting services promoting athletes, and social media wasn’t what it is today.

So I created my own opportunity.

I got back in shape, went to my high school, found my old VHS highlight tapes, had them converted, uploaded them to YouTube, and started emailing college coaches.

Not 10 schools.

Not 50 schools.

Hundreds.

Most never responded.

Some said no.

But a few believed.

One of those schools was Arkansas. They liked my film but told me that because I’d been away from the game, I needed to prove myself at the junior college level first.

Then I got a phone call I’ll never forget.

Coach Hintz from Rochester Community and Technical College (RCTC) in Minnesota had just accepted the head coaching position, taking over for Coach Brad LaPlante, who was leaving to coach back in Texas.

That call changed my life.

I packed everything I owned and moved over 1,000 miles away from home to chase a dream that most people thought was over.

RCTC became one of the best experiences of my life.

I was part of one of the top junior college programs in the country and had the opportunity to compete with and against incredible talent. One of my teammates was Isaac Fruechte, one of the most talented—but even more importantly, one of the most genuine—people I’ve ever met. Watching him eventually make it to the NFL surprised none of us.

Our only loss came in the bowl game against Iowa Western. Their quarterback, Jake Waters, was the best quarterback I’d ever played against. Competing against players like that showed me exactly what the next level looked like.

Looking back, I realize my journey wasn’t really about football.

It was about faith.

It was about resilience.

It was about refusing to let one chapter define the rest of my story.

I had to learn recruiting on my own. I had to market myself, build relationships with coaches, and create opportunities instead of waiting for them.

That’s why I started Clutch Culture Sports.

I don’t promise scholarships.

I don’t guarantee offers.

I help athletes gain clarity, build a strategy, and give themselves the best chance to be seen.

Because I know what it feels like to think your opportunity is gone.

And I also know that sometimes all it takes is one email, one phone call, and one coach willing to believe in you to change your life.

Mine did.

text:
Slogans like "come for vs. come with" collapse the moment you open 2 Thessalonians:

Paul unites them in one event: In 2 Thessalonians 2:1–3, Paul specifically ties "the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to Him" directly to "the Day of the Lord." He uses a single grammatical construction (hyper) for both.

Paul explicitly denies your timeline: Paul states unequivocally that this gathering CANNOT happen until the apostasy occurs and the man of sin is revealed in the temple (2 Thess 2:3). Your theory says it happens before the man of sin is revealed. You are directly contradicting Paul.

The Greek word apantēsis: In 1 Thessalonians 4:17, being caught up to "meet" (apantēsis) the Lord in the air uses the ancient civic term for a delegation going out to meet an incoming king and escorting him the rest of the way in (cf. Matt 25:6, Acts 28:15). It is not an escape hatch to turn around and leave for seven years.

Identical details: 1 Thess 4 (shout, trumpet, clouds, resurrection) matches Matt 24:29–31 (trumpet, clouds, angels gathering the elect after the tribulation).

Slogans aren't Scripture. Paul explicitly chained our gathering to the post-apostasy Day of the Lord. The text stands.

You opened this exchange telling others to "educate yourself" with a movie link, but when confronted with the actual grammar, syntax, and context of the biblical text, you offered only insults, deflections, and unscriptural slogans. Take your own advice: set aside the modern cinema and study the open canon of Scripture with true Berean discipline. The apostolic testimony is complete, clear, and unmovable. This discussion is finished. I wish you well.

text:
Here's a list of internal evidences that this event actually happened:

1.  In the chapter heading, we learn that John introduced himself as:  "John, the same that is called John the Baptist in the New Testament."  This rings true.  I highly doubt that John went around calling himself, "John the Baptist."  To himself, he was simply, "John."  But he did need to clarify to Joseph and Oliver which John he was.

2.  "Upon you my fellow servants, in the name of Messiah..."  This also rings true.  If Joseph Smith had made up this account, he would very likely have John saying, "In the name of Jesus Christ..."  But to John himself - a Jew - Jesus was the Messiah.

3.  "I confer the Priesthood of Aaron..."   This is a perfect example of John using the ancient Hebrew construct state in his speech.  In English, we say, "The Aaronic Priesthood."  In ancient Hebrew, it's "the plates of brass," "the rod of Aaron," "the temple of Solomon", etc. - not brass plates, iron rod, or Solomon's temple.  This is exactly how an ancient Hebrew would have spoken.

4.  "...which holds the keys of the ministering of angels, and of the gospel of repentance, and of baptism by immersion for the remission of sins..."  This is a perfect example of the use of many "and's."  In English, we simply separate complex items in a series by a comma or semi colon.  Ancient Hebrew did not have those punctuation marks.  So complex items in a series were separated by the use of "and" between each one.  This is also exactly how an ancient Hebrew would have spoken.

5.  "...and this shall never be taken again from the earth, until the sons of Levi do offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness."  "...the sons of Levi" is again the construct state.  It's not "Levi's sons."  

6.  Finally, in the above passage, "offer an offering" displays the use of the cognate accusative in ancient Hebrew.  In English, we would say, "make an offering" or "perform an offering."  But in ancient Hebrew, "offer an offering" is a perfect example of the cognate accusative - and is exactly how an ancient Hebrew would have spoken.  

The internal evidence is there in volume - if you only know how to look for it.

Rest in Peace, good boy.

George G. Vest
EULOGY OF THE DOG
September 23, 1870
(Warrensburg, Missouri)

"Gentlemen of the jury.
The best friend a man has in the world may turn against him and become his enemy. His son or daughter whom 
he has reared with loving care may prove ungrateful. Those who are nearest and dearest to us, those whom we trust with our happiness and our good name, may become traitors to their faith.

The money that a man has he may lose. It flies away from him perhaps when he needs it most. A man's reputation may be sacrificed in a moment of ill-considered action. The people who are prone to fall on their knees to do us honor when success is with us may be the first to throw the stone of malice when failure settles its cloud upon our heads.

The one absolutely unselfish friend that a man can have in this selfish world, the one that never deserts 
him, the one that never proves ungrateful or treacherous, is the dog.

Gentlemen of the jury, a man's dog stands by him in prosperity and in poverty, in health and in sickness.
He will sleep on the cold ground when the wintry winds blow and the snow 
drives fiercely, if only he can be near his master's side.

He will kiss the hand that has no food to offer, he will lick the wounds and sores that come in encounter with the roughness of the world. He guards the sleep of his pauper master as if he were a prince. When all other friends desert, he remains.

When riches take wings and reputation falls to pieces, he is as constant in his love as the sun in its journey through the heavens. If fortune drives the master forth an outcast into the world, friendless and homeless, the faithful dog asks no higher privilege than that of accompanying him, to guard him against danger, to fight against his enemies.

And when the last scene of all comes, and death takes his master in its embrace and his body is laid in the cold ground, no matter if all other friends pursue their way, there by his graveside will the noble dog be found, his head between his paws and 
his eyes sad but open, in alert watchfulness, faithful and true, even unto death."

text:
Zack Snyder’s Escape From New York 

The setup is still basically Escape From New York: Manhattan has become a sealed prison zone, the President’s aircraft goes down inside it, and Snake Plissken is blackmailed into extracting him before a deadline. But Snyder’s version quietly mutates into something else. Snake enters the city thinking he is on a simple rescue mission and gradually discovers that every faction in Manhattan has somehow organized itself around intense, highly aestheticized bisexual tension.

Snake himself would begin the movie as aggressively self-contained, almost parody-level heterosexual action iconography: beard stubble, tactical harness, enormous shoulders, speaking in five-word sentences. Then he meets the two people who become his allies: a lethal former mercenary man who is basically Snake’s physical equal, and a glamorous, ferocious woman who runs an underground resistance network from what appears to be the ruins of Studio 54.

And crucially, Snyder would not play this as a joke.

The whole movie would be photographed like a religious awakening.

There would be a scene about 40 minutes in where Snake and the male mercenary have to strip off their soaked tactical gear after falling into the Hudson. They sit opposite each other beside a barrel fire, both shirtless, both covered in rain and blood, saying absolutely nothing. Leonard Cohen plays.

Snake looks over.

The other man looks back.

Cut to a flashback of Snake as a child staring at a fork in a road.

Nobody explains this.

Later, the woman patches up Snake’s wounds. Their faces get very close. Snake looks overwhelmed.

She says:

“You keep acting like you have to choose.”

Snake: “Choose what?”

She looks at him for about twelve seconds.

“Exactly.”

Smash cut to a giant slow-motion explosion.

The President rescue plot continues almost incidentally while Snake’s internal crisis becomes the real spine of the movie. Every major action sequence doubles as a stage in his bisexual awakening.

The midpoint would be some enormous nightclub in Times Square ruled by the Duke of New York. Instead of the original film’s grimy gladiatorial atmosphere, Snyder gives us a decaying cathedral of leather, chrome, fire, and disco lighting. Men dance with men. Women dance with women. Everyone looks like they have been cast from a fragrance campaign.

Snake enters and realizes, with visible alarm, that he is attracted to approximately 90% of the room.

This is the first thing in the movie that genuinely frightens him.

The villain notices immediately.

“Look at you, Plissken. All that armor, and you still don’t know what you want.”

Snake growls:

“I know what I want.”

The villain gestures broadly at the nightclub.

“No, you know what you were told to want.”

Then someone fires a crossbow.

By the third act, the love triangle has become completely explicit, except it is not really a triangle because the two allies are also attracted to each other. Snyder therefore arrives at the revolutionary dramatic structure of a bisexual action polygon.

There would inevitably be a moment where all three are trapped in a subway tunnel while the city floods. Snake thinks one of them has died. He screams the man’s name first.

Then he notices this.

The woman notices that he noticed it.

Snake stares at her.

She says:

“About time.”

He replies:

“Shut up.”

And they resume killing people.

The emotional climax comes after Snake completes the mission. The authorities offer him his freedom and a new identity. Instead, he looks back toward Manhattan, where both of his companions remain.

Government official: “Plissken. Where the hell are you going?”

Snake pauses.

He removes the eyepatch.

His bad eye can now see.

He says:

“Back in.”

Cue Junkie XL.

Daily market brief incoming! **Capital Markets Brief — Thursday, Sept 17, 2026** (post-close edition)

**The five things that mattered most today:**

1. **Post-Fed relief rally.** The S&P 500 rose **+1.2%**, the Nasdaq **+1.7%**, and the Dow **+0.7% (~350 pts)** in the final hour, snapping a three-day losing streak. Saxo called it a "credibility-relief" trade after the Fed reaffirmed its inflation fight. Dow and S&P remain red on the week; the Nasdaq is modestly green.
2. **Bonds rallied too.** The 10Y fell 5.7bp to **4.946%**, back below 5%; the 2Y dropped 3.8bp to 4.688%, with the long end falling faster — the curve flattening continues. "The bond market got there first," as one strategist put it, and now it's nodding approval. But ING warns 5.25% could be next if inflation doesn't cooperate.
3. **US hit Iran's crypto pipeline.** Treasury sanctioned the BitBank exchange run by sanctioned financier Babak Zanjani, accusing it of routing hundreds of millions to the IRGC and processing payments for safe Hormuz transit — part of "Operation Economic Outcast." Separately, the House passed a sweeping sanctions-and-tariff bill aimed at the biggest importers of Russian oil and gas; it now goes to Trump.
4. **Oil kept easing but the war premium is sticky.** Brent −0.7% to ~$105 and WTI near $100 as Saudi crude moved through Oman eased supply fears. Still: US diesel hit a record $6.31/gal, and JPMorgan says it has no clear oil endgame — Brent's "fair value" is ~$90 vs $106 now, with ~10mbd already disrupted.
5. **Crypto joined the rally.** BTC rose to **$76,621 (+0.9%)**, ETH to $2,444, SOL +2% to $100.57. The standout: **Zcash +23% to a record ~$1,369** after Paradigm's Matt Huang disclosed the firm owns ZEC. The dot plot's median 4.1% for end-2026/2027 (one more hike, no sustained cycle) reassured risk assets. Caveat: US spot BTC ETFs shed $296M Wednesday, over $1B in seven sessions.

**Rates & fixed income**
- BOE held 6-3 at **3.75%**, warning Middle East oil could intensify inflation into Q1 2027; UK gilt 10Y fell to 5.205%, Bund to 3.486%. BOJ widely expected to hike Friday. 16 of 18 FOMC members see at least one more hike; October is a ~53% coin-flip.
- Data: weekly jobless claims fell to **196k** (vs 207k expected) — layoffs contained; housing starts −2.6% in August.

**Stocks**
- Generac soared on a deal to sell up to **$8B of generators to Amazon's data centers**; the AI-infrastructure bid is back on. Tech led the rebound; energy lagged with oil.
- Global: Stoxx 600 +0.6% (banks, tech); Asia mixed — Nikkei +0.3%, Hang Seng −0.6%.

**Crypto**
- Broad-based: 94 of 100 CoinDesk 100 constituents higher; small-caps (CoinDesk 80, +4.7%) beat BTC-heavy large caps. $345M in liquidations over 24h — mostly shorts. BTC remains 6.9% below its Sept 4 monthly high of $82,284.

**Commodities**
- Gold: spot +1.1% to ~$4,310 (off Wednesday's six-week low); futures mixed near $4,349. Copper inched up.

**Geopolitics**
- Iran's blockade workarounds are failing: overland costs 4x sea ($12k vs $3k/container), trucks stuck at Pakistan/Turkey borders, Iraq closed cargo terminals; Saudi warplanes pounded Yemen after the Houthis claimed a downed Saudi F-15. Canada is open to the EU's "associate member" offer as the US-Canada trade war deepens.

**Cross-asset volatility**
- **VIX −12% to 15.59**, a two-week low (lowest close since Sept 4) — fear is deflating fast. The dollar snapped its three-day win streak (WSJ Dollar Index −0.1% to 96.07) but sterling hit a 7-week low vs the dollar after the BOE hold.

text:
Indy creators: beware of the efforts of some in the community to normalize that AI gen has to be expensive. It doesn’t.

I only started playing with AI gen because X originally made Grok Imagine free with a free X account. (A smart loss leader for X.) I decided it was worth a $400 a year premium account, which had other X benefits I use frequently. I’m personally opposed to paying for extra renders. I don’t think I should have to pay for beta testing and helping big tech build out market share and infrastructure. My advice for other indy creators is: pick a budget you're comfortable with, monthly, yearly, or per project, and stick to it. 

It’s absolutely reasonable for companies to charge for their services. I’m not a commie. There are big ad agencies and established video professionals who can afford to pay for high-quality AI gen, heavy usage, or better interface options and add-on tools. Let the market decide if they are worth it.

What I object to is the efforts to sucker indy creative types, who have little hope of actually being able to monetize their work (sorry, folks, but it’s true), into spending more than they can afford to chase their dreams. Thick wrapper companies that offer the illusion of helpful tools for $12 a month but simply get access to your credit card to take a piece of the cost of rendering through another provider. Special offers of unlimited renders that turn out to be super limited. Casino-chip credits to make it seem like you’re not spending real money when you are. Too many hopeful creators are getting sucked into spending more than they can afford hoping some short video they make will go viral and make them famous before the credit card is due. (Sorry, folks, probably not going to happen.)

This kind of stuff is not only bad for indy creators, but bad for the industry as a whole. Unlike gambling addicts, there isn’t an unlimited market of people who are going to play a rigged creative game for long. Some small creators will bankrupt themselves and drop out (which doesn’t help anyone), but most of the others will figure out the game and find better ways to play it. They’ll shift from paid online tools to free online ones and they’ll start building tools that work offline. I’ve seen this happen again and again with digital creation over 40 years. Expensive custom computers targeted to artists replaced by cheap laptops. Expensive cameras hyped to indy filmmakers just drove them to figure out how to use iPhones. Expensive editing software drove them to free editing software. Expensive online distribution drove them to YouTube and TikTok.

There is no long-term business exploiting indy creator dreams. I thought that was settled back when MySpace failed. It isn’t a standalone business. Promoting indy creation can be a side business of a larger social network (TikTok), or the focus of a nonprofit community (AO3), or secondary income to serving professionals (see Adobe), but it’s not a profit center.

So whenever I see someone promoting some indy AI gen feature created for “only” 5 million dollars, or a 5 minute AI gen short that looks amazing and only cost 50 grand, I’m highly suspicious of the motivation behind mentioning the budget. If your film is great, great. If your short is impressive, more power to you. But when those are used as examples by others to warn that AI gen is getting more expensive, and people need to accept that, I know I’m hearing spin. Startups that are running out of cash because their business model won’t survive if suckers don’t accept shelling out more money quickly. I can see the end of runways looming.

Long term, AI gen is going to get cheaper, not more expensive. And get better. And most likely simply be a loss leader for X, Meta, Google, and Apple. Or Chinese companies or even El Salvador. The technology is out there. The benefits of mass adoption will bring down costs. Companies will battle for market share by lowering prices.

There will always be a market for enhanced services, extra quality, and heavy usage. But the writing is on the wall. Every ten-year-old will be able to make flying kitten videos for free on their phones, laptops and iPads as just a perk of giving up their consumer data. And if you keep overcharging indy creators, they’ll just use flying kitten apps to create with. Maybe there will be five-second limits, maybe only in 480p, maybe heavily censored, but indies will get around those constraints. And more likely they’ll end up being 4K three-minute AI flying kitten generators in a few years.

As far as bragging about budgets, I have the same point of view about indy films bragging about their budgets. There are two relevant data points: success, budget. I am completely dismissive of anyone who says they made an indy feature film for “only” 800K. Who cares? They can be made a lot cheaper. But if your film grosses over 500M at the box office, like Obsession, damn, that budget is impressive. I want to hear every detail. I’m not impressed that your boutique studio picture “only” cost 10M. Lots cost less. But if it’s Backrooms and grosses $400M worldwide, yeah, I think that’s a really interesting accomplishment.

Anyone bragging about their budget, low or high, in independent film without being able to point to success is irrelevant. Feature films have been made for virtually no budget. So if you make one for 200K I don’t care. Without success you’re just bragging you can spend money. If you mention it cost more than 1M, you’re bragging you can spend investors’ money. I’m not interested. Is it a good movie or not?

The same applies to AI gen features and shorts. If you spend over 100K on an AI feature, and you can’t point to some kind of success beyond it looks cool or professional, I’m not interested in your budget. I’ll decide if it looks cool or professional. If it goes viral or gets bought by a studio, I’d be interested in your budget. For shorts, if you spend more than 5K, I’m not interested in your budget, unless you can point to some measure of success for spending that much on an AI short.

Jenny Krakovsky (@jennykrakovsky) made a feature length AI film for around 5K and publicly documented the steps to do so. So we all know it’s possible. Even without success, I love hearing the details of what cost what, particularly since the clips looked so good. But more important is that the finished work is leading to distribution offers. The metric between those two things is what will ultimately matter the most.

Emily Youcis @AlfredAlfer77, after being a major Sora promoter, and occasional Seedance user, has moved on to open source offline creation and is not only lost forever to online AI services, but becoming a leading advocate of the switch. Can't remember the last time she mentioned a budget on her fabulous (and highly viral) shorts. But I am interested in the details of her costs of moving offline.

If you’re spending a lot of money creating AI video, and have nothing concrete to show for it, any talk about your budget is just telling me you have a lot of money to spend. I'd be more interested in details of where you got the money to waste. Because it doesn’t have to cost a lot to create with AI and no spin is going to fool people into wasting money long term. Any companies counting on costs going up will not survive in the next five years. Either pivot to a smaller number of professionals or find a totally different business model. It was fun while it lasted but indy creators won’t keep writing checks.
