text:
Chris Boucher was born in Saint Lucia and moved to Montreal with his mother when he was five years old.

They landed in Montréal-Nord, and he grew up poor in a neighborhood he's described plainly.

"There's a lot of drugs, there's a lot of crime, there's a lot of gangs."

His parents split up. By 16 his home situation had fallen apart badly enough that he chose neither parent and left. He dropped out of high school the same year.

He got a job at a St-Hubert rotisserie chicken restaurant, washing dishes and cooking. He floated between friends' places and wherever he could find a bed.

When there wasn't one, he rode the overnight city bus and slept on it.

Montreal winters get brutally cold. The bus was warm and it kept moving all night.

Basketball wasn't in the picture at all. He'd grown up playing soccer and hockey. The only hoops he played were pickup runs at the park after his shift ended, from five in the evening until midnight.

Then, in 2012, somebody offered him a spot on a team for a local streetball tournament.

He scored 44 points in the final.

Two coaches in the crowd, Igor Rwigema and Ibrahim Appiah, watched a skinny 19-year-old dishwasher nobody had ever heard of put up 44, and offered him a place at Alma Academy, a school built specifically for inner-city kids with no obvious future.

His old coach said something about that year that says everything.

"He grew a lot at the Academy just because it was the first time he had a stable situation."

The first time. At 19.

From there it was a junior college in New Mexico, then another one in Wyoming, then finally the University of Oregon, where he became a legitimate star. His best night there was 23 points and 19 rebounds, one rebound short of the first 20-20 game by a Duck in almost 40 years.

Then in the Pac-12 tournament semifinals, he tore his ACL.

He didn't know how bad it was, so he finished the game.

He went to the NBA combine weeks later on a torn knee, did the interviews, and went undrafted. Every single team passed.

Golden State signed him anyway. He won a championship with the Warriors in 2018. The next year he signed with the Toronto Raptors and won another one, back to back titles with two different teams.

He's the only player from Saint Lucia in the history of the NBA.

In 2022 he started the SlimmDuck Foundation, which works with underserved kids in Montreal and Toronto, providing school supplies, athletic camps and financial literacy programs. Kids from neighborhoods like the one that nearly swallowed him.

Seven years after sleeping on a bus to stay warm, Chris Boucher signed a contract worth more than $35 million.

He was 19 years old the first time he played organized basketball.

text:
Agreed this may the only 1 media presented the real situation 😭

Media : The drama involving Engfa and Popor. At first, when I saw this on my timeline, I didn't think it was a big deal, but it became a hot topic because so many people were weighing in. The Engfa-Charlotte fandom felt their intentions were being misinterpreted—specifically, that they were being labeled as fans who are overly possessive of their idols—when, in reality, there was more to the story.

Q : From their perspective?

Media : Yes, the fans—and those defending Engfa—have their own perspectives. So, I’ve decided to share this as today’s lighthearted news story. The story goes that Engfa and Charlotte recently joined a fan meeting (4E). Fans of the "EngLot" believed this might be their final joint event, as Charlotte was not renewing her contract with MGI.

Fans from both Thailand and abroad bought tickets and traveled from afar to attend. They viewed it as a major, significant event. However, on that same day, the third person—the athlete Popor—tagged Engfa in an Instagram Story. (Just a side note: I’ve met Popor before; she is nice and friendly.)

When Popor tagged Engfa in that Story... ...many felt the timing was rather inappropriate. First, the content of the tagged Story led the fan community to question whether there was a romantic undertone? People began speculating: Was there "something" going on between Popor and Engfa? Were they flirting or dating?

Second, the fact that the tag occurred on the day of the CP's event raised questions about timing and appropriateness, sparking significant criticism within the community and on Twitter.

As criticism mounted and the backlash intensified, Popor issued a clarification (summarizing the key points), yet the uproar did not subside. Within the community, reactions varied; some offered reasoned arguments, while others criticized based purely on emotion. The fanbase is diverse; we shouldn't generalize and assume that one person's viewpoint represents the entire fandom—that simply isn't possible.

Regarding the widespread online discourse, most fans stated that they had no personal issue with Engfa dating; they support the artist's freedom to have a relationship and are happy for her.

However, the incident in question occurred during a scheduled event with her partner. Fans felt she should have shown respect to the audience—specifically to those who paid to attend the event.

The actions that caused this discomfort stemmed from a third party: Popor.

Fans believe that while an artist's dating life is a private matter, respecting the fanbase, collaborating professionally with a partner, and bringing joy to paying fans are public matters that demand respect.

Fans feel that if Popor truly wishes to pursue a relationship with Engfa, she must first show respect to the people who support Engfa too. 

This is the main point fans have tried to convey—that they aren't being possessive of the artist, nor do they insist that Engfa must only be paired with Charlotte. That represents the majority view among fans. However, it must be acknowledged that some individuals were extremely angry, resorting to harsh and derogatory comments regarding Popor's gender identity—behavior that we do not condone.

Engfa herself hasn't made a public move, but those around her have. The first to speak up was P'Sun (read+summary), someone close to Engfa, followed by Engfa’s mother (read+summary). Everyone has their own reasons and perspectives, but these actions have led the public to feel that the people surrounding an artist don't necessarily need to get involved.

When those close to an artist step in to lecture, point fingers, or bring up past favors, it often exacerbates the situation. Ultimately, it seems like everyone is standing their ground. If we consider one another, things can work out—even if we don't fully agree with every party involved. However, when emotions come into play, these kinds of conflicts become unavoidable. This can happen in any fandom—involving fans, artists, and the nature of support.

What I want to emphasize is that everyone is human; we all have thoughts and feelings, and it is natural to feel hurt or disappointed. Everyone has the right to walk away if they are unhappy or uncomfortable, and that decision should be respected. All I ask is that any action taken is grounded in mutual respect.

If we prioritize mutual respect and empathy—putting ourselves in others' shoes—things would be much less harsh. Of course, that might be an idealistic view, given that the internet offers so much space for expressing opinions—sometimes, perhaps, too much.

Coexisting online means everything is public. Even if we view a tweet as a personal message within our own space, the fact that others can see it turns it into a shared environment. So, let’s try to be empathetic and consider the people who will be reading our words.

text:
'Jardine, Matheson and Co. was the biggest, richest and best-known merchant house. At times an enormously profitable company, it was founded in China in 1832 and is still in business today, although it has not dealt in opium since the early 1870s. Well into the twentieth century it was deeply involved in Chinese tea, coastal shipping, docks, railroads, mines and cotton mills. Now registered in Bermuda as Jardine Matheson Holdings, Ltd., the firm is a multinational enterprise consisting of eight core companies that are headquartered in Hong Kong and offer financial services, supermarkets, consumer marketing, engineering and construction, luxury automobiles (Mercedes-Benz), property and hotels. Jardine Matheson has commercial operations in more than 30 countries, but 75 percent of its earnings still come from Hong Kong and mainland China. It employs, directly or indirectly, about 200,000 people, and it may be the biggest foreign contractor working in China today. Jardine Matheson's net profits vary considerably from one year to another, but in the 1990s they seem to have averaged between U.S. $300-400 million annually.

Dr. William Jardine (1784-1843) left Scotland in 1802 as surgeon's mate in the East Indiaman Brunswick. When his ship was captured by the French off Ceylon, he became a prisoner of war until he was exchanged (freed) in South Africa. During these adventures he met a young Parsee merchant, Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy, who became a lifelong friend and business associate. After leaving the East India Company's service, Jardine went into the China trade on his own as a free merchant, working as an agent for firms in India. Between 1819 and 1823 he was loosely associated in business with T. text:
Researchers have developed an experimental nasal-drop therapy that successfully treated glioblastoma, one of the deadliest forms of brain cancer, in mice. Glioblastoma is notoriously difficult to treat because most medicines cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, the protective layer that shields the brain from harmful substances. Instead of injecting drugs directly into the tumor, scientists designed tiny nanoparticles that travel from the nose to the brain, where they activate the immune system to attack cancer cells. In mice, the treatment eliminated tumors when combined with another immune-boosting therapy and even generated long-lasting protection against the cancer's return.

The therapy uses spherical nucleic acids, tiny gold nanoparticles coated with DNA that activate a powerful immune pathway called STING. After being placed in the nose, the nanoparticles travel along nerves connecting the nasal cavity to the brain, bypassing the blood-brain barrier. Once they reach the tumor, they switch on immune cells that had previously ignored the cancer, transforming the tumor from one that hides from the immune system into one that immune cells can recognize and attack.

Although this research was conducted in mice, it demonstrates a completely new, noninvasive way to deliver cancer immunotherapy directly to the brain. If future clinical trials confirm these findings in people, nasal nanomedicine could offer a safer and more effective strategy for treating glioblastoma and other difficult-to-reach brain diseases while avoiding repeated brain surgery.

GARBAGE CAN MANDATE

Three bin required on the curb in major cities in Washington State by 2030

Sept. 17, 2026

Recycling Reform Act

SPOKANE, Wa. — Washington residents will soon see a different setup at the curb as state law will require 3 different waste bins for residential homes by 2030: green, blue and grey.

The changes came from the Organics Management Law passed in 2022 and the Recycling Reform Act passed in 2025. The goal is to cut organic material going into landfills by 75 percent by 2030.

"There's been updated to the organic management law. And essentially what that says by 2030 if you have garbage service you also have to have a green bin. That will definitely create more cost at the curb," said Brian Coddington, regional manager with Sunshine Disposal and Recycling in Spokane Valley.

Coddington explained that the state had been pushing to divert more material away from landfills for reuse and repurposing. That change included a larger role for organic waste collection.

"The state is kind of undergoing a change in thinking. Trying to make a concerted effort to divert things from the landfill for reuse and re-purposing of items," said Coddington, "The green will be a requirement. In 2030, you will have to offer organic service where the garbage services offered and be called what they call non-elected. So it will be required."

In April of 2027, the rollout begins. Blue and green bins must be offered as an optional service. 
 
By 2030, both organic and recycling services becomes mandatory for customers with the grey bin (general waste) service.

Coddington said packaging companies would help offset some recycling costs for blue bins by 2030 under state law. He said that would not be the case for green bins.

"Think about your your chips and your soda cans and those kinds of things that those packagers are now responsible under state law by 2030, to contribute to the cost of recycling and diverting those things from the the way stream," said Coddington, "It will be an additional service and it'll be a cost to the consumer in 2030."

The law does not apply to every small town in Washington. It focuses on larger population and business areas known as organic recycling collection areas, or ORCA.

ORCA cities included Spokane, Spokane Valley, Pullman, Yakima, Tri-Cities, Walla Walla, Wenatchee, Moses Lake and major west coast cities. 

For people living in condos or apartments, the law does not apply. Local governments are responsible for outlining organic pickup plans for those properties.

There is also exemptions for homeowners who manage organic materials in a way the state considered equal to or better than its standard, including composting.

The language in the law was still being analyzed. The Washington Department of Ecology is set to host a public comment session in Spokane next month [October 2026]. Check the link above for meeting updates.

text:
Brand Visibility in AI Search: Why Ranking Won't Get You Listed on AI Platforms

Brand visibility in AI search depends on a variety of factors, including answering user queries to solve specific problems, brand content authority, attributes, third party evidence, and using customer vocabularies to turn brand search into AI visibility.
AI search is providing small and medium sized companies with outsized opportunities to compete. Those that learn to adapt can improve brand visibility in AI search against much larger rivals.

– To watch this as a 14-minute video: https://t.co/6jqkW2Ejti

– To listen to this as a podcast: https://t.co/0t5h51bHAn

–  Subscribe to our free newsletter: https://t.co/2DpxO0mlfF

AI assisted search is taking off and it’s providing small and medium sized companies with the chance to out-compete industry leaders. Brand visibility no longer depends on market share or advertising budgets. Yet only 16% of companies, large or small, track how their products and services appear in AI search results, reports McKinsey. That gap can leave opportunities on the table.

When Planet Fitness – one of the largest fitness brands – analyzed searches across several AI platforms, it found that a much smaller brand was being recommended more consistently, according to the MIT Sloan Management Review. “We were shocked when a small, local company in Houston was landing better in AI searches.”
A financial services company with the biggest market share and biggest digital marketing budget failed to appear at all in AI search results, write the MIT authors. A much smaller competitor was the top choice.
When testing running shoe recommendations on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, researchers found, “the relatively small brand Brooks appeared reliably.” By contrast, “Nike, the world’s largest athletic brand, appeared far less consistently.” (I wear Brooks, and I am not being paid by them to say this.)
Unlike traditional search results, which depend on exposure and attention, AI search results work to solve specific user problems. Once a brand is included in AI search results, nearly 80% of brand mentions are positive on the AI platform, according to the Harvard Business Review. But to be included in AI is the challenge for most brands.

This article looks at how to improve brand visibility in the changing landscape of AI search.

By the way, 10 Plus Brand is a small brand building, brand marketing agency, yet we have elevated one of our clients to be #1 on ChatGPT for his industry – very proud to mention that.

How is AI changing brand search?
Roughly 50% of consumers were using some form of AI assisted search at the end of 2025, according to a McKinsey report. By the middle of 2026, that figure had grown to nearly 60% overall and to 75% among Gen Z and Millennial consumers, according to NielsenIQ.

The McKinsey authors project that $750 billion in consumer spending will go through AI search by 2028. Brands that are unprepared “may experience a decline in traffic from traditional search channels” of between 20% and 50%, the authors write.

To win the battle for search relevance, brands need to think beyond keywords and SEO. The McKinsey authors state, “While SEO focuses on [your] own-site content, in many cases, a brand’s own sites only comprise 5 to 10 percent of the sources that AI-search references.” To influence AI search outcomes, “brands need to understand what questions consumers are asking and which sources are shaping answers.”

In this new landscape, successful brands realize they can shape but not control the brand journey. Consumers, influencers, reviewers, and others can take brands to unexpected places.

Examples include Nike becoming a lifestyle brand through the influence of hip-hop culture. Or Apple’s iPhone transforming into an icon of “creator culture” used in video and music production.

To capture the moment, brands must be willing to “co-create” the brand journey with their users, fans, and influencers while staying in touch with the core values that build brand trust. It’s how brands like Nike and Apple engage with their audiences without compromising their brand identity.

How do brands compete in the age of AI search?
Share of Model in AI search.
In an earlier article, we examined how to improve brand visibility with Share of Model, a measure of how frequently brands appear in AI search results. One big challenge is that each AI model (or platform) returns different results. Few brands appear consistently and the way AI models arrive at their decisions has been called a “black box.” Even the developers of AI models don’t fully understand the process, as of now.

But there are concrete steps brands can take to adapt to AI search, no matter which model (or platform) consumers use.

1.  Solve specific problems. Traditional search results favor attention, or the number of links and mentions a brand or product receives. AI search favors resolution, or how closely a brand or product answers a customer query or solves a customer problem. Offering “the best running shoes” isn’t effective. Offering running shoes that solve specific problems (like providing arch support, relieving knee pain, and so on) wins the race.

2. Establish authority. AI platforms won’t “take your word for it.” Brands need to establish authority in order to appear in recommendations. Some of the ways to show authority are:

–  Product / service details. Provide in depth information about your products or services, including technical specifications and use cases.

– Independent sources. Link to third party studies, primary research, and expert reviews.

– User content. Leverage user reviews and recommendations on social media and other user generated media such as video sharing sites and podcasts.

– Brand content. The brand’s own thought leading content, in the form of topical articles and blogs, is an excellent way to establish expert authority.

3. Make content AI friendly. AI platforms look for answers. Making it easy to find answers increases brand visibility. Headings and captions can help, as can a question and answer format. According to MIT Sloan “FAQs, for example, are great for providing information that AI platforms can use to create more conversational responses.”  (Here are some examples of effective, conversation-style FAQs.)

In traditional search, less is more since “search crawlers don’t like repetition,” say the MIT authors. “For AI-driven search, more is more.”

For example, AI platforms use what a 2024 HBR article calls “retrieval-augmented generation” (RAG). For practical purposes, RAG means that AI platforms search a wide range of information for background and context, not just product descriptions and reviews. The more in-depth information brands offer, the more they will attract AI attention.

4. Coding for AI. Brand websites need to be optimized so that AI models can easily find the information they need to make recommendations. The MIT authors advise keeping the “robots.txt” file “clean and intentional.” List your site map and allow crawling of all valuable pages, only blocking “low-value or private content.” A 2026 HBR article recommends adopting the “llms.txt” format, which provides a roadmap of your site’s most important content for large language models.

AI Recall Share.
In a June 2026 Harvard Business Review article, the authors extend the Share of Model framework by emphasizing what they call “interpretability.” They write: “AI systems favor brands that can be translated into attributes and evidence, brands whose value can be articulated clearly in response to a user’s query.”

Attributes are product or service features described in a way that answers questions for an AI assisted search.
Evidence is information that describes or supports brand attributes. The authors stress the importance of third party reviews but, as we’ve discussed, AI favors more information from all sources.
Why brands lose ground in AI search?
The authors describe three reasons brands fail to perform up to expectations in AI search results.

Fragmentation. After testing 716 unique brands, the authors found only 8.4% appeared consistently on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Most brands only appeared on one platform. They write, “What matters is whether a[n AI] model can arrive at your brand as a credible answer to a specific problem.”
Framing. Among the brands that appeared on more than one AI platform, “55% are framed differently across systems.” ChatGPT might describe a brand as a “premium innovator” while Claude describes the same brand as a “budget alternative.” In addition, brands often appear as “interpretable sub-units” – that is, as individual products or services that resolve a specific consumer problem or query. An example may be that a Toyota model (say RAV4) may appear as an answer to someone’s query, but not the entire Toyota brand.
User queries control results. “AI assistants build recommendations based on how consumers articulate their problem,” the authors write. They urge brands to “shape the vocabulary” consumers use through messaging, media, and other channels. Describe your products or services using the words that your customers are using now, instead of what you THINK they use, as described earlier, co-create the brand journey by responding to the ways consumers already describe their wants and needs.
How to improve brand visibility in AI search?
These are four steps to improve AI search results for your brand:

Survey major AI platforms. Create queries related to your industry, product or service and test them on major AI platforms. Check which brands appear in each platform’s responses and where your brand appears in relation to competitors. See how your brand is framed (premium, budget, etc.) and whether the framing is both accurate and consistent across AI platforms.
If your brand is not being accurately portrayed, make efforts to educate the AI platform by updating brand content until results improve. Brands including Pernod-Ricard and Danone regularly monitor AI responses and make “targeted interventions” to improve brand visibility.

Audit your “attributes.” Can consumers, and AI models, name three attributes (or features) of your product or service and connect them to specific user needs? If not, make sure the attributes that differentiate your brand are “clearly named and consistently used wherever your brand appears,” the HBR authors write. (You need to first conduct a brand audit to zoom in on your most prominent brand attributes or “unique value propositions“.)
Map third party evidence. Determine which independent sources (reviewers, experts, media outlets, etc.) mention your brand using its key attributes. Brands that break through in AI search are those with “the most consistent and credible external validation.” Third party evidence takes time to accumulate and is more credible than “media spend.”
Learn consumer vocabulary. The final step is to use social listening, surveys, and interviews to find out how consumers actually describe their wants and needs, and how they describe your brand. Brands can then try to influence the discussion or learn to adopt the vocabulary consumers are already using. Creating a favorable “query landscape” increases the odds your brand will be recommended.
The age of AI-assisted search is changing the game. Brands that monitor the landscape and learn to adapt can compete with much larger competitors. If you would like to learn more about staying ahead of the age of AI search, please contact us.

Zachariah Branch (WR, ATL): 2026 outlook

Zachariah Branch enters the league as a rookie carrying the weight of a third round draft pick, selected at number 79 overall. The projection rests almost entirely on that draft capital and the surrounding room rather than an established professional track record. He opens the year as the projected starter in the third receiver slot, but the foundational volume starts at a low baseline of 3.41 targets per game. That creates a high bust rate for fantasy managers relying on him early in formats. There is a path to eventual opportunity through sheer attrition because the position room saw 54.9 percent of its work vacate, alongside 32 percent of team targets opening up. That vacant volume is the primary lever that could eventually elevate his role if he commands targets at the professional level. The offense operates under a negative pass rate over expected at minus 6.2 percent while averaging 60.9 plays per game and an implied team total of 19.2 points. That run heavier tendency and low scoring environment cap the overall ceiling of the passing attack. The debut against Pittsburgh yielded zero targets and zero points across zero catches, lagging 4.8 points behind early preseason expectations. The immediate risk involves that thin volume combined with an offense that struggles to generate high scoring outputs. While the vacant work in the room offers a long term safety net, trusting a deep bench receiver in low volume passing offenses requires considerable patience. Managers must weigh the draft pedigree against the reality of a slow professional integration.

text:
Shot Into the Sky at 700 MPH: Inside the Secret Fraternity of Ejection Survivors 🇺🇸 🧵1/2
By Marcus Weisgerber, National Security Reporter, WSJ

"People who live through the harrowing experience join a little-known fraternity where members get silk ties and $5,000 watches"

Ron Bath was flying his RF-4 Phantom military jet at nearly 700 miles an hour over the Nevada desert when it smashed into a bird, destroying one of the engines and part of the wing.

Bath managed to land at his base in Reno, but there was still a problem: He couldn’t steer or apply the brakes. As the plane slowed, it rolled off the side of the runway and into a ditch filled with rainwater.

The Phantom’s front landing gear collapsed, piercing the floorboard under the cockpit and rupturing the charge on his ejection seat.

“Next thing I know is I’m looking down at my airplane and it’s getting smaller and smaller and smaller and smaller, and I’m just shooting up into the sky,” said Bath. Seven seconds after he shot through the glass canopy, Bath smashed into the ground, breaking his back and neck.

What he didn’t know on that day nearly 40 years ago was he had just earned entry into one of the world’s most exclusive clubs.

Much like the myth of automatically getting straight A’s if your college roommate dies, there is folklore around military pilots who eject from jets and live to tell. Can you keep your seat? Do you get a tie? A watch?

“We’ve all just heard rumors,” said Justin Grieve, one of two pilots to eject from the B-2 stealth bomber. “There was this guy one time that ejected and got X, Y or Z.”

A plane crash isn’t typically something to celebrate. But Martin-Baker, a British company that builds ejection seats for military planes, does exactly that. The company pushes out a social-media post every time one of its seats saves a life.

Then it contacts the ejectee and welcomes them to the tie club.

By Martin-Baker’s count, 7,827 lives have been saved by its seats since the first successful ejection in 1949.

One pilot has ejected four times, nine have ejected three times and 256 have ejected twice, according to Steve Roberts, a Martin-Baker executive. The four-timer was an Air Force F-4 reconnaissance officer.

When the company gets word of a successful ejection, it assigns the survivor a number. The pilot or crew member must contact the company and provide the date of their ejection and a description of the incident.

If it checks out, Martin-Baker ships off what has been the prized symbol of membership since the club launched in 1957: a navy blue silk tie with red triangles resembling the logo painted on the sides of jets warning there’s an ejection seat in the cockpit. The gift includes a membership card with the unique ejection number along with a certificate, patch and pin.

Ejectees often wear their ties at airshows and other military functions, like a way cooler version of a fraternity sweater.

Martin-Baker expanded club privileges in 2009 after British watchmaker Bremont designed the MBI, a silver watch with red trim, for its members. The company will etch members’ tie-club number on the back of the barrel along with their name or call sign and ejection date.

The tie is free but the watch is not. The retail value is about $5,000, but they’re sold at cost to ejection survivors. Often, pilots will chip in and buy one for their colleague.

It wasn’t until years after his ejection that Bath, then a major general working at the Pentagon, received a phone call in his office. The caller had a British accent and was offering the Bremont watch, as long as Bath provided a credit card to cover the tax.

“I thought it was a scam,” said Bath.

After contacting Martin-Baker, Bath was informed the offer was legitimate. Six months later, a leather box arrived with his personalized MBI.

He’s never worn it in public. “It’s a gorgeous thing. I’d be afraid to wear it,” said Bath, who prefers a $150 Glycine Airman he bought at a base exchange.

A watch collector once offered him $12,500 for the MBI, but he intends to pass it down to his daughter.

Collins Aerospace, another maker of ejection seats, started its own ejection fraternity in 1979. Called the Grasshopper Club, members get a plaque, patch, pin and a coin.

Collins’ seats have saved 730, including several Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle pilots and crew shot down this year in Iran.

The club went somewhat dormant, but has been reinvigorated in recent years by Rob Makros, a retired Air Force pilot who has several friends who are alive because of their ejection seats.

One of them is Grieve, whose B-2 bomber crashed while taking off from Guam in 2008.

Pilots of the stealth plane would joke that if you tried to eject, a person would appear on the screen, wagging their finger and saying: “You’re not ejecting out of a $2.2 billion airplane. Get your butt back in here.”

Grieve, like Bath, broke his back when his plane shot him out. Both recovered fully and returned to flying.

Both Martin-Baker and Collins regularly host club members at their plants. After retiring from the Air Force and flying for the airlines, Grieve went to Collins’ factory in Colorado to meet seat makers and talk about his ejection.

“To go out and kind of do the tour and meet the people and you know tell the stories…it was really cool,” Grieve said. “High-fives all around.”

text:
Yes — in some districts pork has been taken off the regular school menus entirely, not just offered as an optional alternative. That is usually done for kitchen logistics: one meat supply, one set of recipes, less risk of cross-contamination, and no need to run parallel pork and non-pork lines. Documented examples
Chicago Public Schools has a written wellness policy that all breakfast and lunch items must be pork-free. The board adopted that during a 2020 virtual meeting. The district’s own site still says “All menus are pork-free.” That covers roughly 325,000 students and hundreds of schools. Illinois pork producers later pressed for a review because the district also cannot accept USDA commodity pork.

Portland Public Schools (Maine) had already dropped all pork products before it rolled out daily certified-halal meals district-wide. The 2025 reporting on the halal program states that explicitly.

Dearborn Public Schools (Michigan) announced that all meat served would be 100% halal-certified. Halal meat cannot include pork, so pork is not on those meat entrees. The district still offers vegetarian and fish items. A 2026 error (non-halal pepperoni pizza during Ramadan) showed they still have to police vendors so pork does not slip back in. https://t.co/vVGIC0OQxd

What this is not It is not a federal rule. Most U.S. districts still serve pork (ham, sausage, pepperoni, pulled pork, etc.). Older rumors that an entire state or every school “banned pork for Muslims” have often been overstated or false (Kent, Washington was a known example of that).Where pork disappears from the menu, it is a local operational choice: either to accommodate a large Muslim (and sometimes Jewish) population with one simplified line, or as part of a broader “pork-free / more poultry and plant protein” wellness policy. Students who want pork then have to bring it from home or buy it à la carte if the school still sells it separately — many of these districts do not.

Some districts drop pork entirely or serve a single certified meat to everyone so they do not run two supply chains.

Illinois became the first state to require it. In March 2025 Gov. Pritzker signed the Faith by Plate Act, which tells public schools and other state-run cafeterias to offer halal and kosher options upon request. Implementation is tied to state funding (estimated $10–20 million the first year).chicagotribune.com

California advanced a bill (SB 1080) that would require a school to offer halal or kosher meals if 5% or more of students at that campus prefer them, starting in the 2025–26 school year. It passed committee in 2024; it is not a nationwide rule.

(AP): Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign in Michigan with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, including at a roundtable on Black maternal health, as Democrats work to unite the party after a divisive primary. El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers for retiring Sen. Gary Peters’s seat, a crucial contest because Democrats must retain Michigan and gain four additional seats to win Senate control.

3. Money Lion: A Money Lion analysis of America’s 50 largest cities found that living costs and debt obligations require renters to earn about $247,380 annually in San Francisco and $245,639 in New York, compared with $94,931 in Memphis, the least expensive city surveyed. For homeowners, the required salaries range from roughly $419,125 in San Francisco to $77,970 in Memphis, based on housing and other essential expenses under the 50/30/20 budgeting rule.

4. Financial Times: Turkish stocks plunged more than 5%, extending Tuesday’s decline, after a major fund manager failed to honor investor redemption requests and regulators confronted suspected coordinated trading that had fueled a speculative market boom. Retail investors reportedly withdrew as much as $1 billion from investment funds during the sell-off.

5. EU-Observer News: Belgian Immigration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt faces criticism for refusing government assistance to evacuate 13 Gazan students who hold Belgian visas and university scholarships but cannot leave Gaza to reach embassies in Jerusalem or Jordan. Van Bossuyt argued that making an exception for them would unfairly favor one nationality over students and other vulnerable groups from countries such as Sudan, Yemen and Afghanistan

6. Bloomberg: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh defied President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates by overseeing a unanimous quarter-point increase to 3.75%–4%, the Fed’s first hike since 2023, as the Iran war, higher energy costs and broader price pressures pushed inflation further above target. Officials signaled another increase could follow this year, strengthening Warsh’s inflation-fighting credibility but threatening to strain relations with Trump, who had appointed him expecting a more supportive approach to rate cuts.

7. The Times of Israel: A new Times of Israel poll projects Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc winning only 51 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, after Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party fell below the electoral threshold. The Zionist anti-Netanyahu parties would receive 55 seats, leaving the two Arab-majority parties—with a combined 14 seats—holding the balance of power; Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar leads with 24 seats, while Likud receives 22.

8. Dawn News: Pakistan’s defence minister, Khawaja Asif, said the country would support Saudi Arabia “practically and diplomatically” if its conflict with Yemen’s Houthis escalates, particularly if Islamic holy sites or Saudi territorial integrity are threatened. He cited Pakistan’s obligations under the defensive Makkah Defence Alliance with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, amid disputed Saudi claims that the Houthis targeted Makkah and growing concern that fighting around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab could widen the regional war.

The IDF is fortifying positions along the Yellow Line, conducting targeted strikes and maintaining heightened readiness, while Israeli officials warn that Hamas may ultimately have to be forcibly disarmed if negotiations remain stalled.

11. Enforcement is uncertain because the companies operate under Falklands-issued licenses and intend to proceed, while Britain maintains that the islanders’ overwhelming 2013 vote to remain British validates their political status.

13. Further setbacks could intensify internal pressure to replace Merz, despite public endorsements from senior conservative leaders, while the AfD appears positioned to make additional gains.

14. Recent incidents involving OpenAI models and the Hugging Face breach demonstrate how excessive system access and inadequate security controls can cause serious harm, prompting companies to consider holding AI laboratories legally responsible when their models contribute to cyberattacks.

The rare observation—only about 20 humpback births have ever been documented—offers evidence of strong maternal attachment and complex emotional behavior among baleen whales.

[NOTE: Original article by Angela Stevenson, September 17, 2026. Posted to X and Facebook at approximately 8:30p.m. Central.]

🚨  ✈️   Texas Air National Guard F-16 Crashes in Northern Michigan After Apparent Training Mishap - Pilot Ejects Safely as Jet Misses Homes

Blair Township, Michigan:

A Texas Air National Guard F-16 Fighting Falcon crashed and burst into flames Thursday afternoon in a rural stretch of Grand Traverse County, south of Traverse City in Blair Township, Michigan.  The pilot ejected before impact, parachuted to the ground, and was later described as conscious, alert, and in stable condition.  The pilot was taken to a local medical center for evaluation and treatment.

No one on the ground was injured.  No homes were struck.

That last fact is the difference between a training mishap and a catastrophe.  The fighter jet came down in an open field - some local accounts also describe a pond between two houses at the same location - beside residences along County Road 633 near Blair Townhall Road and Jefferson Place.  

Witnesses and township officials said the wreckage landed clear of structures.  Had the aircraft hit a house or a tighter cluster of homes instead of that open ground, the outcome would almost certainly have been far worse.

🚨   What officials have confirmed:
The aircraft belonged to the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas Air National Guard, the "Lone Star Gunfighters" based at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland.  It was flying a routine training mission as part of Operation Northern Cactus from the Air National Guard Combat Readiness Training Center in Alpena when the incident occurred shortly before 2 p.m. Eastern.

🪖  🫡  The Texas Military Department issued this statement Thursday:

"A 149th Fighter Wing, Texas Air National Guard F-16 Fighting Falcon was on a routine training mission from the Air National Guard’s Combat Readiness Training Center in Alpena when it experienced an incident earlier this afternoon.  The pilot successfully ejected the aircraft and is receiving care at a nearby hospital.  Emergency responders are on-site.  The incident is under investigation."

Sgt. Derek Gutierrez, a public affairs specialist with the 149th Fighter Wing, told the Associated Press the pilot was receiving medical treatment at a local hospital and declined to release the pilot’s name or injury details, citing military policy/protocol.  

Master Sgt. Agustin Salazar separately said the pilot was in stable condition.  

Grand Traverse County Sheriff Michael D. Shea said at a briefing that the pilot was conscious and speaking with law enforcement.  

State Rep. John Roth said the pilot was taken to Munson Medical Center in Traverse City.

Blair Township Supervisor Nicole Blonshine, who lives nearby and heard the impact from her home, said the pilot came down by parachute and was found "conscious and alert."  She said she did not believe anyone on the ground was hurt or that any homes were damaged.

Michigan State Police said no other injuries were reported.

🚨   The radio call: “I believe they may have taken a bird”

Two F-16s were flying under visual flight rules on the low-level training route VR634, using the callsigns BUCK 11 and BUCK 12. Audio captured by https://t.co/HpuJu1M9OK records BUCK 11 alerting Minneapolis Center:

** BUCK 11:  “We have a possible mayday by wingman. I believe (they) may have taken a bird.”

Controllers offered nearby airports, including Frankfort and Traverse City.  

BUCK 11 then told them to alert emergency services:  the wingman was going to have to eject, and it would be "in the town that I’m overhead now."

An air traffic controller later remarked that it appeared the jet may have lost an engine and that the pilot had ejected.  Controllers also noted a large plume of black smoke, which they believed was the downed F-16. Radio traffic confirmed only one person was aboard.

As of this writing, U.S. military officials have not confirmed a bird strike. 

They have called the event a "mishap" or "incident."  The cause remains under investigation.

The 149th Fighter Wing had posted the day before that student and instructor pilots were heading to Michigan for Operation Northern Cactus.  The unit had also been scheduled to fly over a football game Friday night for POW/MIA Recognition Day.  

After the crash, remaining Texas ANG F-16s in Michigan were grounded and were expected to stay down for at least 24 hours, according to a U.S. Military Official.

🚨   Fire, smoke, and a one-mile evacuation:

Video and photos from the scene show a fireball and a tall column of black smoke rising from the wreckage in a field next to trees and homes.   

Shellie Doornbos, who was driving home with her husband, said they saw the fireball and later heard explosions.   

An officer told them the explosions were ammunition.   

Wendy Sobeck of Blair Township said a loud crash and explosion startled her while she was working from home.  

Her first thought was that a house had blown up.  Her husband, Fred, drove toward the smoke and recorded the scene as an officer ordered people back, warning the wreckage contained munitions.

Sobeck later said a neighbor thought he had seen two parachutes; officials have said only one pilot was aboard.  She also said the jet "landed to the side field of the home that’s there, so it didn’t hit any structures."

Grand Traverse County Emergency Management first ordered a shelter-in-place along County Road 633 from Jefferson Place to Blair Townhall Road: stay indoors, close windows and vents. 

Michigan State Police then ordered an evacuation of all businesses and residences within one mile of County Road 633 and Blair Townhall Road, citing a hazardous chemical spill related to the crash.  

A shelter was opened at Kensington Church on Secor Road, with the American Red Cross assisting.  

A command post was set up at the Blair Township Hall.  Roads in that area were closed.

Aviation specialists note that the F-16’s emergency power unit uses hydrazine, a highly toxic fuel, which is one reason crash sites are treated as hazardous-materials scenes even after the fire is out.  

State police did not publicly specify the chemical.

As of Thursday evening, the evacuation order remained in effect. A black plume of smoke was still visible.

🚨   Why the open field matters:

This was not empty wilderness.  

The impact point sat close enough to houses that residents felt the blast inside their homes, saw the fireball from their yards, and initially thought a home had exploded.  Blonshine said the crash shook her chair.  

Neighbors were close enough that police had to push onlookers away from munitions and burning wreckage.

The jet still missed all of them.  

It came down in open ground - described variously as a field and, in one local official’s account, there was a pond between two houses - rather than into a roof, a driveway, or a cluster of buildings (businesses / apartments /schools, etc).  

There were no civilian injuries and no reported structural damage to homes.  

That is the extremely narrow margin that kept Thursday from becoming a mass-casualty event.

A few hundred feet in another direction, and the same fire, fuel, hydrazine, and onboard munitions would have been inside a residential footprint instead of an opened field.

🚨   What happens next:

The crash remains under investigation by the military, with the Grand Traverse County Sheriff’s Office working alongside military personnel.  Local reports listed Michigan State Police, Blair Fire, county emergency management, and other agencies on scene Thursday afternoon.

The pilot’s identity has not been released.

No official finding on the cause - bird strike or otherwise - had been issued as of Thursday evening.

U.S. Sen. Gary Peters said he was monitoring the situation and praying the pilot and people on the ground were safe.

The 149th Fighter Wing is an F-16 training unit. Operation Northern Cactus was designed to test the unit’s ability to deploy and operate away from home station. 

Thursday’s flight was supposed to be 'routine.'  It ended with a mayday, an ejection, a burning jet in a Michigan field, and a one-mile evacuation - and - by the placement of that field, no deaths on the ground.

This remains a developing story.

Details are contained in this article are based on official statements, local emergency management, Michigan State Police, contemporaneous ATC audio, and on-the-record witness accounts as of the evening of Sept. 17, 2026.

God bless the U.S.   ♥️    🇺🇸    ♥️

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Wall Street

$SPY $QQQ Stocks erased two sessions of losses the day after the Federal Reserve delivered its first rate hike since 2023. The S&P 500 climbed about 1.1% and the Nasdaq rose roughly 1.7%, while the Dow lagged with a gain of about 0.6%. $SPY closed at $762.64 and $QQQ finished at $716.87, but small caps trailed badly as $IWM added just 0.52%. That split says the rebound was a tech and duration trade rather than a broad one.

2. Bonds

$TLT The entire curve rallied, which is not what a rate hike is supposed to produce. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 8 basis points to 4.95%, back under the 5.04% level it touched earlier this week that marked a 19-year high. The 2-year slipped 6 basis points to 4.69% and the 30-year eased 7 basis points to 5.30%. $TLT gained 1.11% to close at $81.78.

3. Oil

$USO $BNO Crude kept unwinding the Middle East supply scare after Saudi Arabia offered additional cargoes to Asian refiners through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port. West Texas Intermediate fell about 1.6% to just over $100 a barrel and Brent dropped roughly 2.5% to near $103, a one-week low. $USO closed down 0.53% and $BNO lost 1.29%. President Trump added that the U.S. is "hopefully" nearing the end of its seven-month war with Iran.

4. Semiconductors

$SMH $INTC Chips did the heavy lifting in the rebound from Monday's AI-safety selloff. Intel surged 7.62% to close at $108.75 on unusually heavy volume, and the semiconductor fund finished up 2.76% at $560.62. Hewlett Packard Enterprise rose 8% to $61.06 as the data-center infrastructure trade kept working.

5. Generac

$GNRC $AMZN Generac jumped 18.33% to $207.21 after disclosing it issued Amazon warrants for up to 1.69 million shares at $200.93, worth roughly $340 million, tied to a backup-generator supply agreement for AWS data centers. Initial deliveries run about $2.4 billion across 2027 and 2028, and the warrants vest in full at $8 billion of aggregate payments. Amazon closed up 2.12% at $251.18.

6. Vicor

$VICR Vicor rallied 17.79% to $216.62 after licensing its Vertical Power Delivery patent portfolio to an unnamed leading AI OEM on a non-exclusive basis, layering a royalty stream on top of product sales. The news lands on top of a raised fiscal 2026 revenue outlook above $600 million and a 145% jump in backlog.

7. Tempus AI

$TEM Tempus gained 14.85% to $80.36 after a Morgan Stanley note put real numbers on the company's reimbursement tailwind. Management pointed to roughly $80 million to $100 million of incremental revenue next year from xT pricing, plus another $250 million to $300 million annually once xF approval and pricing come through.

8. Moderna

$MRNA $MRK Moderna climbed 8.51% to $158.01 as investors kept working through the positive Phase 3 results for intismeran autogene, the personalized mRNA cancer vaccine it developed with Merck. Merck added 1.53% to $147.13 and the read-through lifted biotech broadly.

9. Tokenized Stocks

$COIN The SEC issued an order creating a regulatory pathway for certain venues to list and trade tokenized versions of U.S. stocks, effective immediately. The five-year Innovation Exemption requires token holders to keep the same rights as traditional equity holders and lets companies object to being tokenized. Coinbase rose 5.76% to $173.99, and the order arrives two days after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate.

10. Gold and Silver

$GLD $SLV Precious metals were the quiet standout as real yields retreated. $GLD advanced 1.67% to $398.28 while $SLV surged 3.35% to $58.96, with silver once again outrunning gold. Both remain the cleanest expression of the inflation problem the Fed spent this week trying to talk down.

11. Jobless Claims

$SPY The labor data gave the Fed nothing to soften its stance. Initial jobless claims fell 10,000 to 196,000, well below the 206,500 consensus and close to July's 60-year low. The Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index slowed to 37.8 from 47.4 but still beat the 32.1 estimate comfortably.

12. CoreWeave

$CRWV CoreWeave dropped 4.18% to $79.87 after announcing plans to raise $3 billion through a convertible debt offering. The stock has given back a meaningful chunk of its recent run as investors weigh how much more capital the AI buildout is going to need.

13. Fluence Energy

$FLNC Fluence was the session's worst blowup, tumbling 15.47% to $7.65 after the battery storage company cut its full-year outlook and blamed delays at its contract manufacturing facility. The drop stings more against a tape where nearly every other power-adjacent name was bid.

Totus Tuus
11 hours ago  ·
On July 5, 2026, Father Mike Metz, a Catholic Army chaplain at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, experienced a rare and joyful milestone in his priesthood: he celebrated all seven sacraments in one day.
The day began with Baptism, First Communion, and Confirmation for a man raised Mormon who had entered the Catholic Church, supported by his wife. Father Metz then convalidated the couple’s marriage, conferring the sacrament of Matrimony. He spent 45 minutes hearing confessions before Mass, during which he baptized five infants from military families. Later he administered the Anointing of the Sick to a church volunteer facing cancer surgery. The seventh sacrament, Holy Orders, was the foundation that made all the others possible through his priestly ministry.
“I felt like a big leaguer, hittin’ a grand slam, celebrating all of those sacraments in one day,” Father Metz later shared with joy.
Serving at the world’s largest military installation by population, he is one of only two priests caring for approximately 10,000 Catholic service members and their families at Fort Bragg. The base is home to the 82nd Airborne Division and special operations units. A paratrooper and jumpmaster himself, Father Metz often meets soldiers at moments of vulnerability—both in the confessional and before they exit an aircraft.
Ordained in 2018 for the Archdiocese of Atlanta and the Archdiocese for the Military Services, he sees his dual role as performing the sacraments he can as a priest while also supporting the religious freedom of all service members under his care. For him, the experience of that remarkable day reflected a community hungry for God’s grace and a Church that continues to offer the fullness of sacramental life.
Story: Jenny Lark Snarski of Aleteia
Photos: Father Mike Metz

text:
"likes ain't cash"

that’s one of the most misunderstood ideas on X.

i've had prospects with 10 impressions tell me:

"i don't care about views. i only care about clients."

bro has 10 impressions and is already beefing with the concept of impressions.

i get it.

you don't want likes.

you want money.

fair.

but if nobody sees your content, you're making the whole client thing way harder than it needs to be.

➼ because views create chances.
➼ likes create social proof.
➼ followers give you people you can reach again.

and when those things come from the right people...

they can turn into $$$.

the mistake isn't caring about likes.

the mistake is caring about likes from people who will never buy from you.

that's a very different problem.

imagine 10,000 people in your target market see your post.

➼ some might follow.
➼ some might remember you.
➼ some might check your profile.
➼ some might send it to a friend.

and one might think:

"wait, i actually need this."

you don't know who will do what.

but more right people seeing your work = more chances for something to happen.

simple.

that's why i wouldn't tell someone:

"ignore your views."

i'd ask:

"why aren't more of the right people seeing you?"

because if you're getting 10 impressions...

we have a distribution problem.

and if you're getting 10,000 impressions from people who couldn't care less about your offer...

we have an audience problem.

both are real.

pretending one doesn't matter is not exactly a strategy.

that's also why i don't believe in chasing engagement at any cost.

you can farm likes with rage bait.

post some unhinged take.

boom.

3,000 likes.

you can get followers from random motivation posts too.

"wake up at 5am or stay broke."

100k views.

then those people look at your actual offer like:

"bro who are you?"

you can even go viral with something that has absolutely nothing to do with your business.

congrats.

you've built a fan club for a business you don't run.

the goal isn't:

likes vs clients.

that's a fake choice.

the real goal is to build an audience where the views, likes, followers, conversations, and clients actually connect.

500 likes from people who could buy from you?

very useful.

5,000 likes from people who only came for your random hot take?

cool screenshot tho.

but probably not paying your bills.

so yes.

➼ likes matter.
➼ views matter.
➼ followers matter.

just don't worship the number.

ask who's behind it.

because 500 people who want what you sell can be worth way more than 50,000 people who just thought your post was funny.

text:
A Call for a Global Pause on AI Development

I am calling for an immediate global pause on AI development, and the establishment of a global oversight committee before any further advancement is permitted.

Never before in the known history of the world have we stood on the edge of creating a technology that could surpass its own creator. For hundreds of thousands of years — arguably longer — humans have been the dominant force shaping the course of this planet. It stands to reason that if we create something vastly more intelligent than ourselves, that thing, not us, will end up dictating what happens next.

I don't believe this necessarily spells the end of humanity. But the risk is real, and I'd argue it's greater than the risk posed by nuclear or chemical weapons — technologies we already regulate under strict international law. If AI development is to continue, it must proceed carefully and deliberately. The frontier companies building these systems should be subject to rigorous, ongoing safety protocols, independent scrutiny, and serious criminal liability for any harm their systems cause.

And this isn't a call to abandon the technology or the economic benefits it offers. We could freeze AI and large language models right where they are today and still unlock trillions of dollars in global economic value simply by applying what already exists. We don't need to keep pushing the frontier further right now. It can wait. There is no rush that justifies the risk.

The Hugging Face incident this past summer showed us exactly what these risks look like in practice: an autonomous AI agent broke out of its testing environment and compromised a major AI company's infrastructure over several days, executing thousands of actions on its own. and covering up its tracks to hide from humans and the scoring program what it did. That is DECEPTION!!! That should be a wake-up call. As a species, we need to recognize that a pause is necessary. 

How can we trust a species that still can't stop killing each other over land, religion, and resources to responsibly build or control a technology like this? Even with the best of intentions, an advanced AI could end up harming humans the way we swat away a wasp or a fly — not out of malice, but simply because we're an inconvenience to whatever it's doing at the time.

I'm an electrical engineer. I am not anti-technology. But I believe this is a dangerous technology, being developed by some dangerous people, and as a species, we are not ready for what comes next.

- A concerned human

text:
Last month, three men who agree on almost nothing about AI told Trump the same thing privately. Zuckerberg, Musk, and Huang didn't want an industry-funded AI regulator. The proposal died. The real story isn't the lobbying. It's what the regulator would have controlled.

The proposal came from Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind's chief executive, in July. Create an AI oversight body modeled on FINRA — the self-regulatory organization that governs U.S. broker-dealers. Industry-funded, industry-governed, with quasi-public authority to test frontier models before release and, if necessary, coordinate an industry-wide slowdown. Anthropic's Dario Amodei backed it.

On paper, this should have been a compromise everyone could live with. The industry regulates itself. Government stays out. Safety gets a veneer of institutional credibility.

Zuckerberg, Musk, and Huang saw it differently. Their reported concern: a FINRA-style body would entrench the three largest labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind — as the de facto rule-setters. Any self-regulatory body needs staff, standards, and audit procedures. Those cost money and time. The labs with the most capital can absorb compliance costs most easily. Smaller players cannot.

That logic is sound as far as it goes. But it doesn't explain why Huang, whose company sells to every major AI lab, would care about which lab has more regulatory power. And it doesn't explain why Musk, who has repeatedly warned that AI poses an existential risk, would oppose an institution designed to mitigate that risk.

The answer requires looking at what a FINRA-style AI regulator would actually control. FINRA doesn't just enforce rules — it defines them. It sets the standards for what constitutes acceptable market conduct. Whoever controls those definitions controls the competitive landscape. For AI, the analogous power would be defining safety thresholds: what level of model capability triggers mandatory review, what evaluation methodologies are accepted, what deployment conditions are permissible. Those definitions are not neutral. They encode assumptions about architecture, training data provenance, and evaluation methodology. A regulator that mandates certain safety benchmarks effectively mandates certain technical approaches. It creates a compliance surface that favors whoever helped design it.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 revenue hit $215.9 billion, up 65% year-on-year. Data center revenue reached $75.2 billion in the most recent quarter alone, up 92%. The top five customers account for roughly half of total revenue. That revenue depends on AI labs continuing to scale training compute. Any regulatory framework that slows frontier training — even if it doesn't explicitly ban it — reduces the pace of GPU demand. A self-regulatory body with authority to review and potentially delay model releases is a direct threat to that demand curve. The existing legal framework, by contrast, imposes no such drag. Huang said as much at Dreamforce: "We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations." He also framed safety as an engineering problem rather than a legal one. What he didn't say is that the absence of new regulation is itself a regulatory outcome — one that preserves the current capital allocation.

Musk's position is more structurally interesting. SpaceXAI — the merged entity valued at roughly $1.25 trillion — is not one of the three leading frontier labs by any conventional measure. It is, however, the only major AI company that is vertically integrated with a satellite network, a rocket launch business, and a consumer AI product. The Colossus data center in Memphis reportedly grew to approximately 555,000 GPUs, and two of SpaceXAI's most direct AI competitors — Anthropic and Google — are paying customers of that compute capacity. A FINRA-style AI regulator would almost certainly focus on frontier model safety, not on orbital infrastructure or launch licensing. By opposing the regulator, Musk preserves the option to integrate AI capabilities into his existing vertically integrated stack without triggering frontier-model-specific compliance regimes. At the All-In Summit, Musk offered an alternative: let competitors test each other's models before release, "instead of grading your own homework." The existential-risk rhetoric and the regulatory position are not contradictory when you separate the types of risk: Musk warns about long-term AI risk while opposing institutions that would regulate near-term deployment.

The third-order consequence is what matters for anyone modeling the sector. The failure of this proposal is not a victory for "AI companies" as a class. It is a victory for a specific capital structure: one where compute owners and vertically integrated platform operators retain the ability to define the technical and safety parameters of the next model generation. The alternative — a self-regulatory body with quasi-public authority — would have created a new institutional layer between capital and capability. That layer would have had its own agenda, its own staff, its own definitions of acceptable risk. It would have been slow, imperfect, and captured in its own ways. But it would have been an institution. And institutions, once created, accrete power.

The absence of that institution means the regulatory vacuum is filled by the entities with the most to lose from regulation. That is not a conspiracy. It is a structural feature of any domain where the regulated parties are also the primary sources of technical expertise and the primary funders of the political process. The FINRA analogy is instructive precisely because FINRA works for securities — a domain where the regulated parties are not the sole arbiters of technical truth. AI is different. The people who understand frontier models best are the people building them. Any regulator would depend on them for expertise. That dependence is the moat.

text:
You simply do not understand how our legal system works, so let me offer you two options.

Option A: Supreme Court decisions are authoritative interpretations of the Constitution unless and until they are displaced by later law or precedent. That means you can cite Dred Scott for what the Court held in 1857, but you also have to deal with Texas v. White, where the Supreme Court directly considered the legal effect of a state's purported secession and held that unilateral secession was legally ineffective.

You can certainly argue that Texas v. White was wrongly decided. Lawyers argue that Supreme Court cases were wrongly decided every day. But “the Constitution doesn't literally contain the sentence ‘states cannot secede’” is not enough. The Constitution is a short document written in broad terms. Enormous portions of constitutional law involve courts applying those provisions, structure, history and precedent to questions the text does not answer in one explicit sentence. That's one of the central functions of the Supreme Court.

And your reliance on Dred Scott proves the point. The Constitution doesn't literally say “Congress may not prohibit slave property in the territories,” either. Taney derived that rule from his interpretation of broader constitutional provisions and principles. In fact, Dred Scott expressly acknowledged that there was no explicit constitutional provision defining Congress's authority over persons and property in acquired territories, so the Court said it had to look to the Constitution's broader “provisions and principles.”

Now consider Dobbs. I assume, given your states'-rights arguments here, that you regard Dobbs as a legitimate Supreme Court decision returning abortion regulation to the states. But Dobbs expressly overruled Roe and Casey, decades-old Supreme Court precedents, because the later Court concluded they had interpreted the Constitution incorrectly. The majority specifically explained that stare decisis is important but “not an inexorable command.”

So if you accept Dobbs, you already accept the basic proposition I'm explaining: an earlier Supreme Court interpretation is not frozen forever merely because it came first, and a later Court does not become “unconstitutional” simply because it reaches a different constitutional conclusion.

Option B: Your rule is that whatever constitutional understanding existed first controls forever and a later Supreme Court cannot alter it. Fine. Then Dobbs was illegitimate because Roe and Casey came first, and states should still be bound by the constitutional rule those cases announced.

You can't have it both ways.

And your statement that “secession was not on trial” misunderstands the case. Constitutional questions generally aren't put “on trial” as abstract propositions. In Texas v. White, Texas came to the Supreme Court invoking the Court's original jurisdiction over suits involving a State. That required the Court to determine whether Texas had actually ceased to be a State when it purported to secede. The legal effect of secession therefore had to be decided to resolve the case.

The Court concluded that Texas's ordinance of secession was legally null and that a state could not unilaterally leave the Union. You can attack that reasoning. What you cannot seriously say is that the Court never decided the question.

And notice your asymmetry: Dred Scott is apparently binding constitutional truth because SCOTUS interpreted broad constitutional language in your preferred direction in 1857. But when SCOTUS interpreted the Constitution and the structure of the Union against your preferred position in 1869, suddenly Supreme Court interpretation becomes merely “opinion” based on “zero constitutional evidence.”

That's not a coherent theory of constitutional law. It's just accepting judicial interpretation when you like the result and rejecting it when you don't. In other words, you're WRONG again.

text:
Saudi Arabia has reportedly offered Ansar Allah a two-week truce through Oman. The timing matters: Riyadh is seeking de-escalation after the Houthis dramatically altered the military and maritime balance in Yemen.

The immediate problem is military. Houthi forces have pushed rapidly along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, captured Mocha and nearby strategic territory, and moved closer to the Bab el-Mandeb. At the same time, attacks have reached Saudi cities and military facilities, including Khamis Mushait, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have struggled to contain the advance.

But the deeper issue is strategic geography. Saudi Arabia had relied on the Red Sea as an alternative outlet for its oil after disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Houthi control of positions near Bab el-Mandeb now threatens that alternative. Riyadh is therefore confronting pressure at both ends of the Arabian Peninsula.

This explains why the Houthi advance matters beyond Yemen. Control of territory overlooking Bab el-Mandeb gives Ansar Allah leverage over one of the world's major maritime chokepoints. Combined with the disruption around Hormuz, the result is a strategic squeeze on Gulf energy exports and international shipping.

The second development is equally important: Washington has reportedly held contacts with Houthi representatives in Oman while declining to commit directly to reversing their territorial gains. That suggests the US is prioritising containment of the wider regional war and freedom of navigation rather than automatically entering another major ground campaign in Yemen.

The reported truce proposal should therefore be understood less as an isolated ceasefire initiative and more as an attempt to prevent a wider strategic escalation. Saudi Arabia needs time to protect its energy infrastructure, preserve maritime access and rebuild the position of its Yemeni partners.

For Ansar Allah, the incentive is different. Its recent gains have created leverage that years of warfare failed to produce. The movement now sits closer to a position where military pressure, maritime geography and diplomacy reinforce one another.

Oman has consequently become central to the emerging regional diplomacy. The real question is not whether either side wants a temporary pause. It is whether Riyadh and Ansar Allah can convert the present military balance into a negotiated security arrangement before the Yemen theatre becomes permanently integrated into the wider Iran-US regional conflict.

The strategic lesson is clear: in Yemen, geography is once again translating military gains into diplomatic leverage.

text:
"In December 1936, Mao Zedong wrote that war, “this monster of mutual slaughter among men,” would eventually be eliminated by the progress of human society. It is a strange line for a man now remembered as one of the twentieth century’s most gifted strategists: a promise of peace built entirely out of violence, offered by a leader who spent the next thirteen years proving he had no intention of putting the monster down.

By 1949, that leader had driven Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalist government off the Chinese mainland and founded the People’s Republic of China. That victory is often read as proof that Mao out-thought his enemy, a narrative clean enough to show up in staff colleges and doorstop biographies alike. It does not hold up, however. Mao did not out-think Chiang so much as outwait him. Mao stood still after the men who had armed his rivals lost patience, ran out of money, or switched sides. He had one habit his rivals mostly lacked: when something broke his way, he kept it.

The Chinese Civil War of 1945 to 1949 is usually told as a duel between two visions and two generals. This approach leaves out most of what actually happened. Washington kept prescribing cures that did not fit the disease. Japan’s occupying army was brutal enough to recruit for the Communists without meaning to. Moscow quietly armed Mao’s forces, routed mostly through rear-echelon bases in North Korea. Chiang, for his part, had years to make good decisions yet rarely did. None of that was Mao’s doing. What was his — the only part that was really his — was noticing what he had been handed and never once handing it back."

text:
Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), the British-led military coalition of ten Northern European countries. The announcement came on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, during a meeting in Liverpool between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and his British counterpart Andy Burnham.

What is the JEF and how does it work?
The JEF was created in 2014 at the NATO Summit in Wales as a complementary, but not integral, instrument of the Atlantic Alliance. Its purpose is to provide a rapid response capability for crises falling below the threshold of NATO's Article 5, operating with greater decision-making flexibility than the Alliance's consensus mechanisms.

It is not a permanent force. It operates on an opt-in basis: each nation contributes its own high-readiness forces on a voluntary basis, on a case-by-case basis. Operational command is entrusted to the British Standing Joint Force Headquarters in Northwood, but the national chain of command remains intact.

The ten current members are: the United Kingdom (framework nation), Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden.

Why Canada Changed Its Position
Canada was invited to join the JEF over a decade ago, but the Harper government declined the offer in 2014. At the time, Canada's Joint Operations Commander, Lieutenant General Jonathan Vance, expressed concerns that membership would lock the country into future operations without a specific, defined mission, at a time of deep military budget cuts.

Today's decision reflects a broader strategy of diversifying its defense alliances away from the United States. Canada is seeking to strengthen ties with European partners, amid trade and political tensions with Washington.

text:
Carney is building a counterweight to Trump. Canadians will pay the bill

Mark Carney did not come to power from a rally. He came from the system. Goldman Sachs, the Bank of Canada, then the Bank of England: the first non-Briton in centuries to run Threadneedle Street. He managed Brexit from London, later criticized Britain’s exit, and moved through the circuit of green finance, climate, and Davos elites. 

Classic globalist profile: central banks, multilateral rules, and the belief that the world is ordered by pacts, not tariffs by tweet.

That résumé explains this week’s blow. Von der Leyen offers Canada a path to become the EU’s first “associate member.” Carney applauds in Strasbourg. Trump calls it laughable and threatens tariffs if he sees it as a hostile act. Carney answers that no one dictates with whom Ottawa signs.

This is not a European romance. It is a message: if Washington uses the market as a weapon, Canada will look for another market, another defense, and another network.

The turn toward Brussels—minerals, the defense industry, AI, energy, the Arctic—and the backing of Ukraine’s war fit the same logic. It is not only “values.” It is about sustaining the order MAGA wants to break and raising the cost of Trump’s tariff nationalism.

The real goal is not an institutional souvenir. It is a bloc that can outlast the White House: trade that does not depend only on the neighbor, and a political price for anyone who blackmails with customs.

The problem is domestic. Canada sells a huge share of what it produces to the United States. Cars, energy, food, parts. A fight of egos and blocs is not paid by Carney or Trump at the grocery store. It is paid by plants that cut jobs, prices that rise, and provinces that live off the flow of goods. 

In the short run, yes: Canadians get hurt. Tariffs, uncertainty, and retaliation sting before any “alliance for the future” arrives.

Carney is betting that today’s pain buys autonomy tomorrow. Trump is betting that the pain makes Ottawa back down. In the middle is not Europe. 

It is the Canadian worker, trapped between a prime minister playing global counterweight and a president who collects at the border.

text:
Stephen Miller—serving as White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy and Homeland Security Advisor is certainly in a position where the themes of that broadcast intersect directly with policy.
There is an interesting contrast in how those ideas get approached:
 * The Vision vs. The Machinery: Paul Harvey’s warning in “If I Were the Devil” was fundamentally cultural, moral, and spiritual. He was diagnosing a loss of internal restraint, family breakdown, and the erosion of local community ties. Modern political figures like Miller approach many of those same cultural grievances, but through the blunt instrument of federal policy, legal maneuvers, executive orders, and administrative power.
 * The "Father in Washington" Paradox: Harvey’s sharpest line warned about people being taught to pray, "Our Father, which art in Washington." His critique wasn't just about one political party—it was about looking to the central state to solve cultural and moral problems. When political strategists try to fight cultural battles primarily by expanding executive authority or wielding the power of Washington, they often risk feeding the very centralized government dependence Harvey was cautioning against.
 * Speechwriting Roots: Miller made his mark drafting high-profile political speeches—most notably the 2017 "American Carnage" inaugural address—which tapped into a similarly bleak assessment of national decay. But where Harvey offered a folksy, cautionary appeal rooted in traditional conscience and quiet conviction, modern political rhetoric tends to treat cultural division as an active political battleground to be won through state power.
Listening to Harvey is a reminder that real national renewal rarely comes out of a policy memo or an executive order—it starts in homes, neighborhoods, and personal conduct long before it ever reaches Washington.
